Plibersek indicates support for ban on choking in pornography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:03:00 UTC
11:03:00 KST

Tanya Plibersek says Labor should consider UK-style ban on strangulation in pornography
In short:
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek has indicated support for banning the depiction of strangulation and suffocation in pornography, with some pointing to a similar ban in the UK.
Advocates' calls have intensified following the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl, linked to to a suspected sexual choking act, earlier this week.
What's next?
The government is still consulting on its digital duty of care bill, which could force social media giants to proactively prevent foreseeable harm on their services.
Australia should be "very seriously" looking at banning depictions of strangulation or suffocation in pornography, says a senior Labor minister who has indicated her support.
Advocates' calls for the ban have intensified following the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl, understood to be treated as a suspected sexual choking act.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek highlighted the prevalence of the act during sexual encounters among young people after a 2024 study found that 57 per cent of 18 to 35 year olds have experienced strangulation in the bedroom.
Last year, the UK made it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography showing strangulation or suffocation.
Ms Plibersek said Australia should "very seriously" consider following the UK's decision to outlaw depictions of choking in pornography.
"There is something wrong with a situation where 60 per cent of young people say they've experienced strangulation," she told Insiders on Sunday morning.
"This is not sex education. It's not real life," she added.
Pointing to risks of long-term brain damage or aneurysms in the case of a non-fatal strangulation, Ms Plibersek said there was "no safe way to strangle someone".
NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane added to the calls on Sunday, writing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to ask him to urgently introduce the ban.
"When pornography depicts an act capable of causing brain injury, unconsciousness or death, it should not be treated as just another form of adult entertainment," she wrote.
Ms Sloane said young people were being exposed to sexual violence online without understanding the danger of the behaviour.
"We cannot wait until another family is living through a tragedy before we take seriously what our children are being taught by pornography."
It is an issue found in other online content, with a 2024 study demonstrating that on average young boys are served extremely misogynistic content within 23 minutes of downloading social platforms, such as TikTok and YouTube shorts.
Ms Plibersek acknowledged the role that social media algorithms played in perpetuating harmful narratives online, following a push by advocates for the government to introduce laws that make algorithms opt-in only.
Among them is Teach Us Consent founder Chanel Contos, who urged the government to take the issue more seriously.
"I think it's quite obvious the harm that algorithms are doing to everyone, but particularly young people, and women are largely on the receiving end of that," Ms Contos told the ABC.
"And I think that something that has 71 per cent of Australians supporting it should be taken as a serious policy proposition."
Ms Plibersek said there were ongoing discussions about how that would look in practice, but remained open to an opt-in model as the government continued to consult on its upcoming digital duty of care bill.
The issue was also front and centre earlier in the week, when national cabinet acknowledged rates of intimate-partner homicide and sexual violence remained "unacceptably high", agreeing on priorities for the next five-year plan to tackle the issues.
Smart glasses moratorium considered
The federal government is also closely considering a moratorium on the import of smart glasses, which can be used to discreetly film people without their consent.
The devices look like ordinary glasses and yet allow the wearer to record images, video and audio, mostly surreptitiously, with the press of a button.
The Greens, with the support of some crossbenchers, have called on the government to halt the import of such glasses as well as as other wearable recording devices for at least 12 months, until tougher privacy protections are passed into law.
Ms Plibersek revealed the attorney-general was due to deliver an update on the government's position shortly, as she labelled any use of the glasses "really troubling".
"If they're going to be used, there should be safeguards around how they can be used," she said.
"I mean, it's already possible, I believe, to buy glasses where you can disable the filming light, so it's not apparent that they're filming as they're being used. That is really, really troubling".

Ukraine targeted Russian facilities used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones in the occupied city of Donetsk, as well as in the village of Hvardiiske near Simferopol in occupied Crimea, according to the General Staff.

‘Green miracle’: US teacher returns to China after 26 years to find donation grew into forest
‘You gave the trees life and watched them grow, just as parents take pride in their children,’ says Sakolsky
A retired American teacher has reunited with a Chinese farmer 26 years after their initial encounter, returning to the once-barren sandy landscape transformed by his generous donation into a lush green environment.
In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, now 67, was teaching English in Luoyang, Henan province, central-eastern China, when he discovered Inner Mongolian farmer Yin Yuzhen’s efforts to combat desertification. Inspired by her dedication, he donated US$5,000 to support her mission.
The pair first met during a donation ceremony in the Mu Us Desert in 2000. Afterwards, Sakolsky returned to the US, while Yin used the funds to plant over 50,000 trees.
Today, vegetation covers more than 80 per cent of the Mu Us Desert, which is one of China’s four major sandy regions.
In May, Yin, now 60, reconnected with Sakolsky via video call and invited him back to China to witness the “green miracle” that his contribution had helped foster.

A tiny, oily fish is TikTok's latest obsession. Is there a catch?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:01:07 UTC
11:01:07 KST

In Brief
- A social media trend known as "sardinemaxxing" has seen sardines cleared from supermarket shelves after hot demand.
- Experts say the social media trend could be dangerous for other fish.
Walk down the canned fish aisle at your local supermarket right now, and there's a good chance you'll find a gap where the tinned sardines used to be, as a viral TikTok trend sends a wave of new fans in search of the small, oily fish.
The trend, dubbed "sardinemaxxing", has seen influencers push sardines as a beauty and wellness must-have, with some calling them "Botox on a fork" for their purported skin, hair, and anti-ageing benefits.
But experts say the trend raises real questions about where those sardines are coming from — and what happens if the hype spreads to other seafood.
Why groceries are going viral
Sardines are just the latest grocery item swept up in a social media-driven buying frenzy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Cottage cheese and Greek yoghurt both had their moment in the past year, part of a broader "proteinmaxxing" wave prizing high-protein foods.
Lisa Asher, a retail and supermarket expert at the University of Sydney Business School, said the pattern is driven by a mix of influencer culture and wellness trends.
"What bothers me isn't that the kids are eating sardines … it's that they're taking advice now from people who are probably not people you should be listening to," Asher said.
"It's a new form of advertising with a lot of unknowns — we don't really know who's paying who and how much they're making out of it. That is a problem.
"In magazines, we used to look at celebrities, but celebrities have been replaced by influencers."
She said the trends all follow a similar pattern: demand increases, the product goes out of stock, prices sometimes rise, and eventually, when the hype cools down, it comes back in stock.
"But this is a product that is made from fish in the sea," she adds. "We don't want to overfish because suddenly, then we have none."
The big catch
That's where the environmental risks come in.
Adrian Meder, sustainable seafood program manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, says history shows a sudden cultural appetite for a particular seafood can do serious damage — pointing to shark fin soup, sea cucumber and some tuna fisheries as species pushed towards collapse by surging demand.
"We've yet to see online popularity as a driver of major declines in our oceans, but a cultural surge in popularity of a seafood has time and time again decimated populations of species from tunas, to sharks, to abalone, to sea cucumbers," Meder told SBS News.
"Online popularity is clearly capable of producing massive changes in consumer demand."
There's also a traceability problem: much of the tinned sardines on Australian shelves is imported, and it can be difficult to know where a can came from or how sustainably it was caught.
Jonathan Smart, an affiliate senior research scientist at James Cook University, agrees that origin matters.
He co-authored a study, released last week, that found Australia ranked just 52nd in seafood production, despite having about eight million square kilometres of fishing waters.
"The fisheries that a lot of our imported seafood comes from are actually quite unsustainable — and Australia imports a lot of seafood when perhaps it shouldn't," Smart told SBS News.
"By importing so much seafood, we're essentially exporting our environmental footprint to other countries that don't have the same level of management that we do."
He worries a viral trend like this one could make that problem worse.
"If a trend like this is popping up and all of a sudden you've got greater consumption of a species, the fear I would have is that then is going to lead to, again, a greater surge in that imported seafood.
"We just don't know if that's going to have the same sustainability levels as if you were actually consuming something locally."
A resilient little fish
But of all the species to go viral, sardines might be one of the best placed to handle their 15 minutes of fame.
Smart says sardines are a fast-growing, short-lived species with rapid turnover, making them naturally resilient to heavy fishing.
Because changes in biomass are driven more by environmental conditions — like ocean upwellings — rather than fishing activity, sardine and anchovy fisheries are some of the biggest in the world, he said.
"They can actually provide a really, really big harvest from them normally under sustainable conditions, depending on the fishery that they're coming from."
Locally, there's also a genuine opportunity: Australia's biggest fishery is a sardine fishery in South Australia — a fact Smart says is little known because much of the catch goes to aquaculture feed.
"Very little of it actually goes to human consumption," he said. "That's why I often recommend to people that we should be eating more sardines because that is a really sustainable fishery.
"We catch a lot of fish from it, and there's a lot of opportunity."
Meder agrees that there's room for Australians to put more sardines on their plate.
"Some cultures, including many Australian communities, actually used to eat a lot more sardines than they do now," he said, pointing to a shift in seafood consumption to more environmentally vulnerable, less abundant, and expensive fish species — of which trends like these could help reverse.
But that only holds if the sardines on the shelf are actually Australian — which means consumers may need to check labels and do a bit of Googling before putting them in their shopping basket.
So while sardines may be getting the limelight for just a brief period before scrollers move on to the next trend, if there's anything we can take from it, it's that the humble little sardine is actually built for this moment.
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

Human-wild animal clashes on the rise in China’s Giant Panda National Park
Farmers on the giant nature reserve report rising concerns over damage to crops and livestock as well as attacks from wild animals
Friction between humans and wild animals at China’s Giant Panda National Park intensified significantly over the past decade as conservation efforts expanded, a new study has found.
Farmers reported increasing losses between 2015 and 2024 stemming from damage to property and crops as well as attacks on humans and livestock.
The team behind the study said the issue had become the most prominent challenge facing the park’s administrators.
The Giant Panda National Park covers 22,000 sq km (8,500 sq miles), two and a half times the size of Yellowstone in the United States, and officially opened in 2021.
The park, which spans the provinces of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, is now home to more than 1,300 wild giant pandas, 70 per cent of the total population.

JD.com’s US$1.3b expansion could test Hong Kong’s footfall-driven retail property model
Chinese e-commerce firm builds network of stores and warehouses that analysts say may reduce reliance on footfall for some retailers
JD.com’s rapid expansion in Hong Kong could challenge the property model that has long made the city’s busiest streets and shopping centres its most valuable, analysts say.
The investments are part of a broader push into Hong Kong by JD.com, which in June said it had invested HK$35 billion in the city across retail, logistics, technology and other businesses.
For decades, Hong Kong property values have largely been driven by location: the more people passing through a street or shopping centre, the higher the rent it could command.
Analysts said JD.com was testing a different model. Its stores, warehouses and logistics facilities were valued not only for the income they generated, but also for their role in a wider network moving goods to customers.

Mr Wale fiercely criticised China's recent ballistic missile launch and has made it clear he is uneasy with China's security role in Solomon Islands — although he has not tried to tear up the 2022 agreement the Pacific nation signed with Beijing.
He also announced not long after taking power that he had agreed to kick off negotiations with Australia on a new treaty — with officials racing to complete the discussions by the end of this year.

NASA’s Roman telescope set to launch on cosmic mapping mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
01:50:00 UTC
10:50:00 KST

NASA’s Roman telescope set to launch on cosmic mapping mission
WASHINGTON - NASA is preparing to launch its new flagship space telescope on Aug 30, embarking on a multi-year mission to create an unprecedented map of the cosmos and shed light on some of the biggest mysteries in physics.
Designed to take a panoramic view of the vast reaches of space, the Roman Space Telescope “will help unlock the secrets of the universe,” US President Donald Trump said on Aug 28 during a ceremony at NASA headquarters in Houston, Texas.
Standing over 12m tall, the state-of-the-art observatory is scheduled to launch from Florida at 7.26am (7.26pm Singapore time) aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
Developed over more than a decade at a cost topping US$4 billion (S$5.09 billion), the telescope is named after pioneering US astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, who became known as the “Mother of Hubble,” another of NASA’s flagship telescopes.
While Hubble revealed that the universe is expanding faster than previously thought, Roman will seek to answer some of the other unsolved mysteries, including those of dark matter and dark energy.
“Roman will give the Earth a new atlas of the universe,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said in April when he unveiled the project to the press.
With a field of view more than 100 times larger than Hubble’s – and significantly wider than James Webb’s – Roman will survey vast swaths of the sky from a vantage point 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, which it will take about 100 days to reach.
Designed to work in tandem with other observatories such as Webb, which offers greater power and precision, Roman aims to discover thousands of exoplanets as well as tens of thousands of supernovae, the explosive deaths of massive stars.
“It will be the biggest catalogue of astronomical objects anybody’s ever produced, and it will help us understand how common are solar systems like our own,” Dave Content, Roman’s technical manager, told AFP.
The new telescope will also shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in physics: dark matter and dark energy.
Their origins remain unknown, but together they are believed to make up about 95 per cent of the universe.
Dark matter is thought to act as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the universe’s expansion.
With its infrared vision, Roman will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago, effectively looking back in time and offering scientists a glimpse into the universe’s distant past and helping them better understand these two mysterious phenomena.
Surprise
Roman’s observations will complement the work of the Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid probe, and are highly anticipated because they could challenge scientists’ understanding of the universe’s structure.
Julie McEnery, Roman’s senior project scientist, said recent research suggests the way scientists have been thinking about the universe’s early expansion, based on the predictions of existing models, may be wrong.
“Recent observations hint that our standard model of the universe is incorrect,” she told a press conference on Aug 29, adding that Roman will help clear that up.
“It will definitively say, ‘Yeah, the model works, or it doesn’t.’ And if it doesn’t, it’s going to provide us with the precision and quality of data that will allow us to start to distinguish between those options.”
Scientists and the general public will have access to all of Roman’s data.
But the sheer volume will be daunting, Content warned.
The telescope will be generating about 1.3 terabytes of data a day, “which means you basically can’t download the data to anybody’s laptop,” he said.
For McEnery, the more data, the better.
“I very much hope, and in fact expect, that the most exciting science from Roman will be a surprise, something we couldn’t predict, and that will set the stage for the next deeper set of questions for future missions to address.” AFP

Australia could make social media algorithms optional and follow UK ban on pornography depicting strangulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
01:49:30 UTC
10:49:30 KST

The Australian government is considering allowing users to opt in or opt out of social media algorithms, and is looking at a recent UK ban on depictions of strangulation and suffocation in pornography.
The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said social media was “playing a huge role” in the increase in sexual violence among teenagers and choking, and confirmed the options were being considered as the government develops its second action plan to end family and domestic violence against women and children.
It follows the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney after a suspected sexual strangulation act. Guardian Australia reported on Thursday that a source informed about the case said the teenager was believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, often referred to as “choking”. No arrests have been made.
Plibersek told the ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday that social media algorithms are deliberately feeding boys and men violent content and normalising strangulation during sex.
“If you set up a social media account as a young boy in Australia today, it takes an average of 23 minutes for you to be fed misogynistic, violent misogynistic content online. That is a deliberate decision of the social media companies that is wrecking our young boys, giving them all of the wrong ideas about what healthy relationships look like,” Plibersek said.
“It is no coincidence that 60% of young people now report that they’ve experienced strangulation during a sexual encounter … It is pervasive and widespread and deadly, and it’s being fed to our young people and normalised.”
Chanel Contos’s Teach Us Consent has campaigned for algorithms to be opt-in only on social media.
Plibersek said the government was working with the group and considering how to potentially design an opt-in or opt-out system for algorithms.
“We’re absolutely up for work on algorithms. Opting in to those recommender algorithms that are causing so much harm, opting in or opting out,” she said.
“We’re also, of course, looking very closely at the recent Meta case in the US [and] the moves that the UK government have introduced to prevent the depiction of strangulation and suffocation in pornography. These are all really important considerations as we develop our next action plan on family domestic and sexual violence, so that work’s going on right now.”
The government legislated a ban on social media for under-16s which took effect in December, and has also introduced age-verification for pornography. But Plibersek has previously conceded children were easily able to dodge the new rules.
Labor will also soon begin consultation on a digital duty of care bill that will put the onus on tech companies, including AI companies, to make online spaces safer for all users.
Plibersek said the digital duty of care legislation, as well as a second round of privacy reforms, could also help tackle camera-equipped smartglasses, which she said she had serious concerns about.
“Tech companies should know that their products are safe and make them safe before they release them on to an unsuspecting public. I know the Attorney-General has asked the privacy commissioner to look specifically at these glasses,” Plibersek said.
“We’ve got a second tranche of privacy legislation coming up soon as well … things like this that can be used to furtively film, including during sexual encounters, for that filming then to be made public or used against someone who is being filmed as a way of blackmailing them, I am very concerned about the potential uses of these glasses.”

BERLIN, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Borussia Dortmund's new Greek duo Konstantinos Karetsas and Giannis Konstantelias made an immediate impact as Niko Kovac's side opened its Bundesliga campaign with a 2-0 home victory over Hamburg on Saturday.

Dortmund next face fifth-tier HEBC Hamburg in their rescheduled German Cup first-round tie, while Hamburg host Mainz in the Bundesliga.
"We were pushed too deep in the first half and once Dortmund get into their rhythm, you are always chasing them. ====================================================================================================

Xinhua Commentary: How the SCO is raising the bar for better global governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:45:59 CST
10:45:59 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- The world is facing a growing crisis of global governance. Protectionism, unilateralism and power politics are throttling international cooperation just as mounting global challenges demand it most.
Against this backdrop, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at last year's "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting, calling for a more just and equitable system of global governance.
The SCO offers a practical answer. Over the past 25 years, it has demonstrated how countries with different political systems, development paths and civilizations can work together.
Guided by the Shanghai Spirit of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations and pursuit of common development, the SCO's 25-year practice offers a vivid illustration of the five principles of the Global Governance Initiative -- adhering to sovereign equality, abiding by international rule of law, practicing multilateralism, advocating the people-centered approach, and focusing on taking real actions.
These principles are reflected in the SCO's increasingly institutionalized cooperation across a wide range of sectors. With regional security and stability at the heart of its original mission, SCO countries have committed themselves to long-term good neighborliness, friendship and cooperation based on equality, consultation and respect for diversity.
The establishment of four new security-focused centers demonstrated the SCO's emphasis on translating multilateral consensus into concrete action. Cooperation among SCO countries has helped thwart more than 1,400 terrorism- and extremism-related incidents in the past 25 years, while the organization has conducted over 40 joint counter-terrorism exercises and operations.
The SCO's approach to security also reflects a broader understanding among SCO countries that lasting security cannot be separated from political trust, economic development and people-to-people exchanges.
The launch of seven China-SCO cooperation platforms covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, higher education, vocational and technical education, and artificial intelligence further underscores the emphasis on shared development with people-centered outcomes.
Through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and closer alignment of development strategies, SCO members have seen positive momentum in both foreign trade and intra-SCO commerce. Calculations based on World Trade Organization data showed the total volume of goods imports and exports of the ten members reached about 8.88 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025.
Projects such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Silk Road e-commerce service hub and the SCO university network are further turning connectivity into tangible benefits, making it easier for people across SCO countries to travel, trade, study and access broader economic opportunities.
People-to-people exchange activities have also become an important pillar of SCO cooperation. Through institutionalized dialogue and expanded interaction, differences in history, culture and civilization can be turned into sources of mutual understanding and cooperation.
Beyond the region, the SCO has played an active role in upholding the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and international law, contributing to the settlement of regional and international issues and promoting coordination among multilateral mechanisms.
The SCO Plus format has further broadened the space for dialogue among the Global South, facilitating exchanges in governance experience and practical cooperation.
Over the past decades, the SCO has shown that diversity need not lead to division, and that countries with different political systems, development paths, and civilizations can cooperate on equal footing without butting heads.
Looking ahead, the SCO is well positioned to bolster high-quality regional development and contribute more wisdom to building a more just and equitable global governance system. ■

Musk calls OpenAI bosses ‘untrustworthy assholes’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
01:01:24 UTC
10:01:24 KST

Musk calls OpenAI bosses ‘untrustworthy assholes’
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has branded OpenAI bosses “utterly untrustworthy assholes” after the company announced plans to withdraw its artificial intelligence models from Cursor following the coding platform’s acquisition by SpaceX.
Musk, who co-founded OpenAI in 2015 with its current CEO Sam Altman, President Greg Brockman, and several other developers and researchers, left the company three years later over its direction and has since been locked in a bitter public and legal feud with its leadership.
Earlier this month, SpaceX completed its $60 billion acquisition of Anysphere, the developer of Cursor, which provides programmers with access to AI models from several companies.
On Friday, OpenAI abruptly announced that it intends to end Cursor users’ access to its models, with a “proposed shutoff date” of November 12. The company said it could not be confident that “SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk’s companies violating contracts.”
I couldn’t care less. Scam Altman and Greg Stockman are utterly untrustworthy assholes who stole an open source nonprofit.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) August 29, 2026
“I couldn’t care less. Scam Altman and Greg Stockman are utterly untrustworthy assholes who stole an open source nonprofit,” Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
OpenAI models account for about 5% of Cursor’s user traffic, according to co-founder Michael Truell, who said the company was in talks with OpenAI to resolve the dispute. He noted that Cursor had been one of OpenAI’s earliest customers and said it had trusted the company’s platform to remain “neutral infrastructure” for its business.
OpenAI said its agreement with Cursor allows it to cancel the contract within a limited period following a change of control, although it has not accused Cursor itself of violating its terms.
Anthropic, one of OpenAI’s main rivals, quickly moved to capitalize on the dispute, saying it would increase computing capacity to support its Claude models on Cursor following the cutoff announcement.
Musk, who initially invested an estimated $38 million in the venture, sued OpenAI in 2024, alleging that he had been misled into funding it on the understanding that it would remain a nonprofit. The company, now valued at about $850 billion, has since restructured, with its nonprofit parent retaining control of and a stake in its for-profit arm, which operates ChatGPT.
During court proceedings, Musk accused OpenAI of breaking that founding commitment by adopting a profit-driven model and accepting a $13 billion investment from Microsoft. The billionaire has repeatedly accused Altman of having “stolen a charity” and described himself as a “fool” for providing the company with early financial support.
In May, a US federal jury rejected Musk’s claims, finding that he had waited too long to bring the case and had missed the statutory deadline. Musk has pledged to appeal the verdict.

Scott turns back clock in Tour Championship title tilt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
00:52:34 UTC
09:52:34 KST

In short:
Australian Adam Scott is in a tie for third in the PGA Tour Championship.
Scott is three shots back from leader Viktor Hovland.
What's next?
The final round of the Tour Championship will be held on Sunday (Monday AEST).
A much-craved second major continues to elude him but Adam Scott may be one great round from capping his decorated career with a second season-ending Tour Championship title.
As golf's biggest names jostle for the $US10 million ($A14 million) winner's cheque in Atlanta, Scott quietly but steadily climbed into a tie for third place entering the final round.
The 2006 champion compiled a classy third-round five-under-par 65 at Atlanta's East Lake Golf Club to position himself three shots behind Norwegian leader Viktor Hovland.
With his own 65, Hovland turned a halfway share of the lead into a one-shot buffer over American Ryan Gerard (66) as he reached 15 under.
So often cruelling his winning chances on the greens, putting was for once Scott's saving grace on Saturday (Sunday AEST).
The former world No.1 drained 132 yards worth of putts, including near 25-footers for three of his six birdies on the eighth, 13th and 17th holes.
It was Scott's second-best putting round of the year and presented the 2013 Masters champion with an enticing opportunity to land first PGA Tour victory since February 2020.
"It's a good spot," Scott said.
"Within striking distance. It's so congested, though. It's going to need a really great round, I think. There's someone lurking who's going to have that."
Min Woo Lee, Australia's only other player in the elite 30-man field for the $US40 million showpiece, remains an outside hope of becoming the first Tour Championship debutant to win since Xander Schauffele in 2017.
Lee is equal ninth after carding a third-round 66, but will need to reel in a raft of superstars.
At 12 under, world No.1 Scottie Scheffler (66) shares third spot with fellow American Chris Gotterup (67), Scott and Swede Ludvig Aberg (65).
Rory McIlroy was the biggest mover of the day, a round of 63 vaulting the world No.2 from 23rd to joint seventh with Cameron Young (68) at 10 under.
Then it's Lee and American trio Russell Henley (66), Jacob Bridgeman (66) and Sam Burns (67) all at nine under.
The 46-year-old Scott is relishing his crack at another big title.
"I can kind of stick with my game plan of being fairly conservative at least for the front nine," Scott said.
"And if I can execute that, then maybe I've got to start flag hunting a little bit and being a bit more aggressive than I have been.
"But I'll try to play that by ear when I'm out there. It's fun to be in the mix for the Tour Championship and the FedExCup."

Trump Promises His Venezuela Oil Deal Will Lower Gas Prices. But When?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
00:29:20 UTC
09:29:20 KST

President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States has entered a “historic” deal with Venezuela, saying that it gives the U.S. majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. Calling it the “BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY” in a post on Truth Social, he said that the agreement would “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans.”
The Trump Administration has long expressed an interest in Venezuela, which boasts the world’s largest proven crude-oil reserves as of 2023—approximately 303 billion barrels, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
But the President did not outline how soon, exactly, Americans can expect to feel relief at the pumps. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment on the expected timeline.
The answer is especially relevant amid the ongoing war with Iran. One of the linchpins of the conflict is a Tehran-imposed blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil had previously passed. The move has been consequential for the global economy. In the United States, the national average cost for a gallon of gas is $4.08 as of Saturday, according to the AAA, as compared to $3.20 one year ago.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the deal a “huge win” for America in a social media post on Friday, saying that it means “lowering gas prices here at home.”
Any eventual decline in gas prices could provide relief at a time when Americans are already contending with persistent inflation, which was the focus of remarks made by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming on Friday.
However, it could be a while before the impact of the new deal with Venezuela is directly felt.
What we know about Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
Much of what is known about the deal comes from a statement released on Telegram by acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez late Friday.
“It provides for the development of 17 strategic fields, with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels of oil, more than $100 billion in investment and more than $209 billion in tax revenue for the state,” the statement said. “These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere and greater stability in international markets.”
Despite its vast oil reserves, the country only produced about 1.1 million barrels per day in July, according to a secondary-source estimate from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
The EIA has attributed Venezuela’s long-term production decline largely to “government mismanagement, international sanctions, and the country’s economic crisis,” which contributed to “a lack of investment and maintenance in the energy sector and a deteriorating infrastructure.” The agency found that Venezuela’s total energy production declined by an average of 8.2% annually between 2011 and 2021.
“The U.S. deal with Venezuela is very important strategically,” says Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist at Rystad Energy. “The new wave of investments that is about to come to Venezuela as a result of this deal will be crucial to turn around the country's aging oil infrastructure. Venezuela will be able to increase its production at a faster rate and unlock barrels that would otherwise have stayed underground.”
The agreement envisions private operators playing a central role in that effort. Rodríguez’s post explained that the agreement allows Venezuela to increase its oil production “through the participation of private operators,” without further elaboration.
A State Department official tells TIME that Rodríguez has granted a private company, which is “a joint project of the U.S. government and an experienced private operator in Venezuela,” 100-year rights to develop the fields, adding: “This new entity will be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco.”
The deal would give the U.S. 55% of the new company’s effective output, “split between equity ownership and guaranteed at-cost off-take,” the official says.
Although they declined to comment on the expected timeline for these steps, the official adds: "As the company scales production, the resulting stable supply of at-cost oil in our Hemisphere will go toward filling the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve and fulfilling the supply needs of our Great U.S. Military.”
Other key factors also remain unknown—including how the deal will be financed and whether it includes any target dates for achieving various outcomes.
Why gas prices won’t lower immediately
One of the main reasons that Americans are unlikely to see immediate relief from high gas prices is that the deal is linked to 17 oil fields in Venezuela, not access to 65 billion barrels of already-produced crude oil.
While those fields contain proven reserves, Venezuela does not have the infrastructure in place currently to produce the oil at a rate that would significantly and rapidly affect the wallets of everyday Americans.
Such concerns arose after former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was ousted by the United States in January, when oil executives and analysts assessed the viability of developing the country’s reserves.
Speaking at the White House on Jan. 9, ExxonMobil Chairman and CEO Darren Woods called it “uninvestable,” given his assessment of the “legal and commercial constructs—frameworks—in place today in Venezuela.”
“There's an opportunity in Venezuela with all the resources there,” he said. “We don't have that challenge of finding; we have the challenge of developing those resources.”
Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy/PDI, provides a similar assessment. He tells TIME, “While the hope of lower gas prices sounds promising, it still will take billions of investment to get that oil.”
In her statement, Rodríguez said the initiative is expected to “facilitate a significant flow of investment aimed at the recovery and reconstruction of strategic infrastructure for the development of our hydrocarbons industry.”
But it remains unclear where that investment will come from, including whether the private operator will provide the financing and how the project will proceed “at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” as Trump said.
De Haan also questioned whether the agreement’s unusual structure could discourage investment. “How can the U.S. lay claim to a sovereign country’s natural resources?” he says, adding that even with approval from Venezuela’s acting president, a 100-year contract could face legal challenges or prove difficult to enforce.
“That may slow down oil companies from wanting to invest in Venezuela,” he explains.
And financing is only one hurdle; the physical work required also shapes the timeline.
“Drilling and pumping that oil will take a very long time. Changes to fuel prices won’t happen overnight or even in months,” De Haan says, adding that global refining capacity is currently constrained, further limiting the speed at which additional crude supply could affect the market.
Galimberti says that consumers should expect a long road between the initial investment and the ultimate production and distribution of oil.
“You will need to factor in several quarters and, in quite a few cases, years,” he says. “Therefore, it is a deal whose benefits will be seen mostly in the medium-long term.”
“To lower gasoline and diesel prices in the short term, the most effective way by far is by increasing the flows from the Middle East,” Galimberti says. He points to recent successes in bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, including pipelines and ports being developed across the Gulf.
Even without potential legal hurdles from within Venezuela, executing on the promise of the reserves could take years, which means that Americans may be in for a wait before they see the impact at gas stations across the U.S.

China offers aid package for Nepal

China's package of assistance to Nepal is being implemented, including emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid, with some relief supplies set to arrive in Kathmandu soon, said Foreign Minister Wang Yi during his phone conversation with Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal on Saturday.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that a severe mudslide disaster, triggered by a sudden glacier collapse in Nepal's border area, has caused significant casualties and left people missing on both sides. It has been the most serious cross-border disaster between the two countries in recent years, and the relief efforts are unprecedentedly complex and arduous.
He said that China attaches great importance to the situation. President Xi Jinping immediately issued important instructions, setting clear requirements for rescue and emergency response work. Premier Li Qiang traveled to the disaster-hit area to guide the work on the ground.
Wang said that while urgently carrying out rescue and relief efforts on its own side, China extended a helping hand at the earliest opportunity and supported Nepal in its emergency disaster relief efforts.
Xi has sent a condolence message to Nepali President Ram Chandra Poudel, and Li has expressed condolences to Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, Wang noted.
China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit area in Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation, according to a meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee. This is an important political decision made by China and demonstrates China's friendship with Nepal, he said.
Wang said that two teams of Chinese tunnel rescue experts had rushed to the disaster-stricken area and Kathmandu to offer assistance, and China has shared with Nepal important information such as images, satellite and hydrological data of the disaster-stricken area, including early warning information of the upstream barrier lake.
He said that for Nepalese citizens stranded on the Chinese side, China has made proper arrangements and will assist them in returning to Nepal as soon as possible, expressing his gratitude and hope that Nepal will continue to assist and transfer Chinese citizens in Nepal.
Wang said that China and Nepal are a community linked by mountains and rivers and sharing a common destiny. In the face of the disaster, the two countries should stand together firmly, join hands to deal with it and overcome the difficulties together, and interpret the traditional friendship across the Himalayas with concrete actions.
Shisir conveyed condolences from Nepali leaders to the Chinese government and people and to the families of the victims, and expressed sincere gratitude for China's emergency humanitarian assistance.
He said that although both Nepal and China had been hit by the disaster, China had overcome its own difficulties to extend condolences and provide assistance to Nepal at the earliest opportunity, fully demonstrating the high level of Nepal-China relations.
   
The Nepali side once again expressed its gratitude to China and will continue to work closely with China to make every effort to rescue Chinese nationals who remain stranded or unaccounted for, while jointly working to locate and rescue missing foreign nationals, he said.
Nepal stands ready to strengthen cooperation with China in areas such as post-disaster reconstruction, disaster prevention and mitigation, and climate change response, and to further advance the strategic partnership of cooperation between the two countries, he said. (Xinhua)

Turkiye, Somalia forces free cargo vessel hijacked by pirates
Somali authorities say 14 pirates were killed in the 10-day operation to free a Cameroon-flagged cargo vessel.
Turkish and Somali forces have freed a cargo ship held captive by pirates off the coast of Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland state, according to authorities.
In a statement on X on Saturday, the Somali Ministry of Defence said that “14 pirates” died in the operation to free the Cameroon-flagged MV Latuf.

Four of their boats were also destroyed, it said.

The rescue operation was conducted under a defence cooperation agreement between Somalia and Turkiye, aimed at strengthening maritime security, protecting Somalia’s coastline and combating piracy, it said.
The Somali Defence Ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the wellbeing of the ship’s crew.
A local elder, Abdullahi Warsame, from the Jiifle community in the Godob Jiraan district of Puntland’s Nugal region, told The Associated Press news agency that the vessel and its crew had been freed.
The MV Latuf left the Turkish Port of Tekirdag in late July. It was hijacked on August 17 in waters off the coast of the Nugal region of Puntland, a semi-autonomous federal state in northeastern Somalia.
According to the Marine Traffic website, the cargo ship has continued its voyage to its reported destination in Dar-es-Salaam in Tanzania.
Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somalia in the 2000s, peaking in 2011, before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.
But attacks have surged since April, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year, the highest since 2013, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization. At least five cargo ships have been held hostage, the last of which was seized on August 20 off the coast of Yemen.

Online anti-Muslim backlash collides with different reality in South Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
00:06:30 UTC
09:06:30 KST

Online anti-Muslim backlash collides with different reality in South Africa
Online anti-Muslim rhetoric is growing, but life on the ground tells a more complicated story.
Nquthu, South Africa – When Zwelibi Jack Ngubane died at the age of 105, he had already made one thing clear to his family: he wanted to be buried as a Muslim.
Hundreds of family and community members gathered for his funeral in Nquthu, a rural part of northern KwaZulu-Natal where Christianity and traditional African beliefs are dominant and Muslims are a tiny minority. Ngubane had converted to Islam late in life after observing the faith of his young grandson.
When he died, his family honoured his wishes. His funeral was conducted according to Muslim burial rites before he was laid to rest in the family burial plot in his village. For a community largely unfamiliar with Islamic burial practices, the funeral was a novelty.
But it wasn’t a controversy. That distinction has become increasingly important in South Africa.
In recent months, anti-Muslim rhetoric has become more visible online, intersecting with a heated national debate about immigration and anti-migrant movements. Posts have accused Muslims of attempting to take over South Africa, questioned their belonging in the country and accused Muslim organisations of using charity and poverty to convert Black South Africans to Islam.
One social media post complained that humanitarian organisation Gift of the Givers had been “getting on our nerves with their insistence on pushing their Muslim beliefs in South Africa”. Another claimed: “Most foreigners in South Africa are Muslim and if you look most countries experiencing war are Muslim countries not Christian ones.” Others have accused Muslims of “targeting poverty-stricken communities and converting them to Islam”.
But in the rolling hills and villages of Nquthu, the picture is different.
For Samukelisiwe Ngubane, her first encounters with Muslims came through Indian shopkeepers in a nearby town. “We have never had a problem. Some people are curious about what they [Muslims] do, but there have been no problems,” she told Al Jazeera.
When her brother, Khethukuthula Dlame, converted to Islam in 2012 as a teenager, it was hardly an issue. Dlame, now 26 and one of only a handful of Muslims known in his village, is familiar enough to his neighbours that his Islamic clothing is a source of teasing rather than hostility. One neighbour jokes that he wears a dress.
“In these communities, there’s harmony and respect. People really respect my religion,” he told Al Jazeera, standing alongside his grandfather’s gravesite.
The contrast raises a question: is South Africa experiencing a rise in Islamophobia, or is social media making a marginal phenomenon appear much larger than it is?
A small but old community
Muslims make up a small minority in South Africa. The country’s 2022 census counted less than one million Muslims, or approximately 1.6 percent of the population. South African Muslim leaders give higher estimates, with some putting the country’s Muslim population at between two million and five million people.
But Islam’s presence in South Africa stretches back centuries. Muslims came to the Cape through several routes, including enslavement and political exile, from parts of Asia and the Indian Ocean world under Dutch colonial rule from the 17th century. Muslims were already present at the Cape before the arrival in 1694 of Shaykh Yusuf of Macassar, a Muslim scholar and political exile.
Today, the community includes descendants of enslaved Muslims brought to the Cape centuries ago, South Africans of Indian ancestry whose families have lived in the country for generations, Black African Muslims, converts and more recent migrants.
Dlame believes attempts to mobilise people against Muslims are not primarily emerging from rural communities.
“The move to orchestrated hate towards Muslims is not at a community level. If you’re looking at people when they’re mobilising, it’s not people from the villages. It is people in cities and in hostels.”
“The people behind this understand the flash points. If you really want to cause divisions, you use tribal rhetoric and the people you mobilise and agitate are in hostels because the living conditions are not good.”
South Africa has repeatedly experienced outbreaks of xenophobic violence since the end of apartheid, with migrants from elsewhere on the African continent often bearing the brunt. The question is whether some of that anti-migrant rhetoric is also being directed at Muslims.
‘No widespread Islamophobia’
Thembisa Fakude, a South African political analyst and journalist who is Muslim, told Al Jazeera that fears of widespread Islamophobia are being overstated.
“I’ll argue that there is no widespread or any orchestrated, well-planned Islamophobia directed towards Muslims. We don’t have that.”
He acknowledges anti-Muslim rhetoric online, but argues that it should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that South African society itself has become Islamophobic.
“It’s true, but it’s not only South Africa. This is global … In South Africa, yes, it’s true. You find that there will always be bigots, you know, and others will be, you know, ultra-Zulu nationalist or ultra-nationalist.”
Fakude also argues that Muslim communities need to confront allegations of racism and exploitative labour practices within their own ranks rather than characterising every criticism as religious prejudice.
“It is a storm in a teacup. And I think what’s concerning me is this othering by Muslims wanting to position themselves as victims and taking this course by themselves. It’s extremely dangerous.”
What starts online does not always stay there
Muslim religious leader Moulana Sulaiman Ravat told Al Jazeera that, while ordinary South Africans are largely not Islamophobic, he is more cautious about what could happen next.
“At the same time, I think on the ground, South Africans in the main are not Islamophobic, and there’s a variety of indicators to substantiate that.”
But Ravat warns that online rhetoric can influence attitudes over time.
“I don’t think we can go to the other extreme. We must understand that there are certain global political realities, and the Islamophobia project aligns with those global agendas. And therefore, if we become complacent or nonchalant about it, what people are exposed to online could start impacting their psyche and how they think.”
Ravat argues that Muslim identity is sometimes being presented as evidence that a person is somehow less South African. For him, the premise is false.
“I would think I would say they are deeply religious and deeply patriotic, and there is no contradiction between the two.”
His own children, he said, are fifth-generation South African Muslims of Indian heritage.
“They don’t speak the language any more. They are as South African as anyone else.”
Two South Africas?
Back in Nquthu, Islam does not arrive through a social media algorithm. It arrives through a neighbour, where Dlame’s mother cooks a halal meal for this reporter and other guests. Earlier, at a community meeting, Dlame explained that Muslims, too, believe that Jesus was a prophet of God. Ordinary villagers listened attentively and joined in Zulu melodies in praise of God.
For now, the distance between the online conversation and life in communities such as Nquthu remains significant. But Ravat says that does not mean the possibility of deeper hostility should be dismissed.
“Better be proactive than reactive. It’s a global reality. It has been for the last 20 years. And the fact that it could increase in South Africa and could have serious consequences, you could argue, is unlikely but not impossible.”

In April, US President Donald Trump threatened that Iran’s “whole civilization will die” unless Tehran agreed to Washington’s demands. Trump has since repeatedly issued similar threats, saying that US forces could obliterate the country’s civilian infrastructure, including power plants and bridges.
Appearing on Carlson’s show on Friday, Kent described the nuclear option as realistic, saying that “we would be fools to think that this couldn’t happen here, in this current scenario, especially as the [Trump] administration scrambles for a way out.”
How close are we to nuclear war? According to Joe Kent, a lot closer than you think.

He noted that Trump has failed to achieve any of his constantly shifting objectives in the conflict with Iran, despite employing the whole gamut of US military and economic capabilities.

The US abruptly suspended its most recent wave of strikes on Iran late last month, amid media reports that the Pentagon has largely depleted its stockpiles of high-precision munitions and interceptor missiles.

Several days later, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled a slew of new sanctions against Tehran, targeting nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions, including 21 based in China.

Voting closes in Iceland’s knife-edge EU referendum
Iceland’s leadership has promised to honour whatever the country’s people decide.
Voting has closed in Iceland’s referendum on resuming membership negotiations with the European Union.
Voting stations closed on Saturday, but it could take several hours for a clear victory for either the “yes” or “no” camp to emerge.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

The referendum does not have exit polls, and ballot counting only began once voting stations closed.
Polling suggests the vote is on a knife-edge, with different surveys putting either side narrowly ahead, but none straying more than a few points from an even 50/50 split.
The vote comes 13 years after Iceland, then led by a Eurosceptic government, paused EU accession talks.
The country is currently governed by the pro-EU Social Democratic Alliance, which called the vote and promised to honour whatever the Icelandic public decides.
If Icelanders vote “yes”, the country would likely start years of negotiations with Brussels to hammer out membership terms. It would then hold a second referendum on whether to formally become part of the EU.
Security, the relatively sluggish Icelandic economy, and the future of the Icelandic currency, the krona, have all been significant themes in the run-up to the vote.

In short:
Storm Hunter has become the only active Australian tennis player to enter all four grand slams as a qualifier.
Hunter will play her first US Open since 2023 when the New York grand slam begins on Monday.
What's next?
Hunter is one of six Australians playing on Monday.
There is a very good reason why facing big-hitting French Open and Wimbledon semifinalist Marta Kostyuk in the US Open first round holds no fears for late-blooming Australian trailblazer Storm Hunter.
The 32-year-old has just sent tennis officials scrambling through the record books after qualifying for the Open's main draw for the first time.
Historians could only confirm Hunter is the first active Australian player to successfully qualify for all four grand slams, a rare feat few others from anywhere have accomplished.
Hunter did not do it easily, taking out compatriot and great mate Maddison Inglis in her first match, fending off two match points in her second and waiting through a 24-hour weather delay to advance with a third straight sudden-death victory.
"This is the last slam on my list to tick off to get through qualies and coming in I hadn't played many singles matches in the last few months so, yeah, it feels amazing," Hunter said.
Having missed more than a year after rupturing an Achilles tendon, Hunter is back in the Flushing Meadows main draw for a first time since 2023.
Her "reward" is a first-round tussle on day one with the 11th-seeded Kostyuk, who is coming off charges to the last four at both Roland Garros and the All England Club.
"Yeah, it's tough," said the one-time world number one doubles ace.
"She's obviously having a really good year. She's a great player, very physical with the way she plays and a really good competitor.
"So it's going to be tough. Obviously a very quick turnaround from playing qualifiers to my first round tomorrow, but I'm feeling good and she's the one who's under all the pressure to play against me and I have practised with her before.
"I know what her level is and I know it's going to be a challenge, but I'm up for a challenge. It's going to be fun. I'm going to enjoy it.
"There's been lots of times in my career I didn't think I'd be back playing at this level, so to be back in the main draw of a slam is awesome, and I'm just going to go out and enjoy it and give it a good crack."
Hunter is among six Australians playing on Monday.
Kim Birrell faces Petra Marcinko, Talia Gibson also plays a Croatian in veteran Donna Vekic and fellow rising star Taylah Preston takes on American Alycia Parks.
Adam Walton, up against China's Yibing Wu, and Aleksandar Vukic playing Japan's Rei Sakamoto are the only Aussie men in first-round action.
Sixth seed Alex de Minaur opens his campaign on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week

Unknown Publisher

Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
This is the 27th time since Russia invaded Ukraine that the Zaporizhzhia plant has had to rely on emergency diesel supplies.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in southeastern Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week, the world’s nuclear energy watchdog has warned.
The plant, which Russia has occupied since 2022, is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Zaporizhzhia’s mayor says Russian advance reaches city’s outskirts
- list 2 of 3Russia reports Ukrainian drone strike near Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
- list 3 of 3Russia warns it could target UK in response to Kyiv firing British missiles
The plant needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool and has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the IAEA said in a statement.
“The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has not had a delivery from an off-site storage facility in about six months but was supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA said.
The Vienna-based agency is now trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines.
Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. It has not generated electricity since September 2022, over six months after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year, but the plant’s reactors must be kept cool to prevent a meltdown of the fuel inside.
“This is the 27th blackout at the plant since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion,” Ukraine’s deputy head of military law enforcement, Gyunduz Mamedov, wrote on X on Saturday.
The IAEA has had a permanent presence at the site since September 2022, after Russia took control of the Ukrainian facility in March that year.
Both sides in the conflict regularly accuse the other of attacking the site, which sits on the banks of the Dnipro River and demarcates the front line in the sector.
On Friday, the IAEA said there had been three incidents that week with drones at the plant, injuring two employees. It did not say who launched the drones.
Earlier this month, a drone strike close to the plant killed one nuclear specialist and wounded 17, with Moscow asserting that Kyiv was behind the attack.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that Russian actions in and around the plant constitute nuclear blackmail against Ukraine and Europe more widely.
In 2024, footage emerged of a fire in one of the power plant’s cooling towers, prompting Ukraine to accuse Russia of nuclear blackmail.

'RSS vision is to see the world as one': Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat at New York event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
23:19:46 UTC
08:19:46 KST

'RSS vision is to see the world as one': Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat at New York event
Edited by: Prisha Patnaik / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 30, 2026, 06:35 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
'Unity in diversity in Bharat's DNA: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat
NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat, addressing around 5,000 members of Indian-American organisations at Madison Square Garden in New York, spoke about unity, pluralism, individual responsibility and the obligations of the Indian diaspora, while arguing that material success alone cannot define a fulfilling life.Bhagwat was speaking at the “Universal Oneness Celebration”, organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue. He framed his address around the idea of “oneness”, drawing parallels between the pluralism associated with the United States and what he described as Bharat’s “unity in diversity”.“When we say America, United States of America, one word is often discussed frequently. That is pluralism,” Bhagwat said. “And when we say Bharat, another word, another phrase is discussed: unity in diversity.”“For Bharat, this unity and diversity, both are in their DNA,” he said.Bhagwat said differences between people were a natural feature of life, but argued that these differences existed alongside an underlying sense of oneness.“So many styles of living. We appear different. We are different,” he said, pointing to differences in people's everyday needs and circumstances.
“But there is innate oneness. That is why we feel for each other,” he added.He described diversity as the “decoration of oneness”, presenting unity not as the absence of differences but as something that exists beneath them.Bhagwat also linked this idea to what he described as the responsibilities of individuals, societies and nations. Nations, he said, should not be seen merely as geographical entities but as having a larger purpose.“These nations are not merely geographical entities. In the design of this universe, nations have to carry out a duty,” he said, quoting Swami Vivekananda's formulation that every nation has a message, a mission and a destiny.
‘Be true to America’: RSS chief message to diaspora
Turning to the Indian diaspora in the United States, Bhagwat said Indians living abroad had a primary responsibility towards the country where they lived and worked.“So we are Americans, and we should be true to America,” he said.He described this as a duty towards one's “karma bhumi” — the land where a person lives and works.“The diaspora, Indian diaspora, they have a duty to their karma bhumi. They must fulfill that. They should be loyal to their karma bhumi,” Bhagwat said.At the same time, he said Indians abroad could maintain a connection with Bharat as their “janma bhumi”, or birthplace, and could contribute to the country if they wished to do so after fulfilling their responsibilities to their adopted home.“But it is not obligatory,” he said.Instead, he said, the connection with Bharat should be reflected in the values carried by the diaspora.“Your janma bhumi expects you to live the values it has imparted on you,” Bhagwat said.Bhagwat also questioned the idea that professional success should be measured primarily through earnings and material possessions.“How much we earn is not important. How much we distribute is important,” he said.He asked whether a career could be reduced to money and material happiness, while acknowledging that material aspirations had a legitimate place in Hindu philosophy.“You think of career? Is career only money? Is career only material happiness?” Bhagwat asked.He referred to the four Purusharthas, saying that Artha and Kama represented important material dimensions of life alongside spiritual pursuits.“It is not denied. In four Purusharthas, Artha and Kama are two important Purusharthas related to material life,” he said.Bhagwat also referred to the traditional four stages of life — Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa — arguing that people acquire different responsibilities as they move through life.“So you have to learn, you have to sustain life, and you have to give the advice, your experience to next generation,” he said.He argued that material abundance by itself could not guarantee fulfilment.“So the material happiness is transient, cannot satisfy,” Bhagwat said. “And if abundance of material happiness is there, it may fail also. And therefore there is no satisfaction.”
Highlights responsibility towards others
Bhagwat's broader argument centred on the idea that human intelligence carried with it a responsibility towards others.Using the example of a hungry person watching someone eat, he said people instinctively recognise another person's suffering and cannot simply ignore it.“A simple experiment you can do, or I can challenge you to do. When you are taking your lunch or dinner, let a hungry man stand before you, and let him stare at your full platter with hungry eyes,” he said.“You can try; you will not do. Because we are human beings.”He contrasted human beings' ability to think and plan with the instinctive behaviour of animals, but said the ability to think also brought a responsibility to use that capacity correctly.“If you think in the right way, you go nearer to God. If you think in the wrong way, you go nearer to the animal kingdom,” he said.
Bhagwat offers interpretation of Dharma
Bhagwat also offered a broader interpretation of “Dharma”, saying it should not be understood simply as religion or worship.“Dharma is not religion. It is not worship. It is beyond all this,” he said.He described Dharma as a sustaining principle that allows people and society to manage competing aspects of life and maintain balance.“It is the balance which sustains everything at once, simultaneously, and simultaneously everyone can progress,” Bhagwat said.He similarly argued that progress should not require either individuals or society to be suppressed.“Individual, society and environment, they have to proceed together, progress together,” he said, adding that different aspects of an individual's own life — body, mind and intellect — also had to advance together.
Bhagwat concluded by returning to the idea of responsibility towards both one's place of work and birthplace.He called on people to fulfil their duties towards their “karma bhumi” as well as their “janma bhumi”, saying such an approach could help a world struggling with multiple challenges.“To that destiny and fulfill our duties in our karma bhumi as well as our janma bhumi,” he said.“If we do that, that will be a boon for the world struggling with all these problems and stumbling at every step.”
Prisha Patnaik is a journalist with The Times of India, writing across geopolitics, international affairs, culture, history and internet culture. With over two years of experience in social media and digital content, she is interested in how news, politics and culture are shaped for digital audiences. She holds a master’s degree in Media and Communications from Goldsmiths, University of London.

The US could gain control over part of Venezuela’s oil reserves for 100 years – The Telegraph
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:05:43 EEST

The US could gain control over part of Venezuela’s oil reserves for 100 years – The Telegraph
Kyiv • UNN
The US is discussing control over Venezuela’s 65 billion barrels of reserves for 100 years. More than $100 billion is planned to be invested in the oil industry.
The United States could gain control over a significant share of Venezuela's oil reserves for 100 years under a major agreement that U.S. President Donald Trump called "the largest oil deal in world history." The Telegraph reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the agreements provide for long-term U.S. control over Venezuela's oil fields, while the American side could receive rights to use them for the next 100 years.
This concerns control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. That is more than one-fifth of Venezuela's total proven reserves, estimated at approximately 303 billion barrels and considered the largest in the world.
The agreement is designed to last for decades
The agreements cover 17 strategic oil fields. Private companies are planned to be brought in to develop them, while investment in Venezuela's oil industry could exceed $100 billion.
Trump said the agreement would more than double the oil reserves available to the United States and, in the long term, help lower fuel prices for Americans.
At the same time, the detailed legal and commercial terms of the agreements have not yet been disclosed. In particular, it remains unclear in exactly what form the United States will obtain long-term rights to Venezuela's oil fields and how the 100-year control mechanism will be implemented.

Nepal is warning that the danger of new floods will persist until both lakes have completely drained. Meanwhile, rescuers continue searching for people under the rubble after the disaster, which destroyed border infrastructure and resulted in a large number of deaths and missing people.

Ontario’s Doug Ford prods Trump with sign rejecting ‘Lake America’ name

Ontario’s Doug Ford prods Trump with sign rejecting ‘Lake America’ name
The ‘Lake Ontario’ sign comes in response to the US president’s efforts to rename the body of water ‘Lake America’.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has unveiled a new – and very blue – response to United States President Donald Trump’s controversial order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
On Saturday, Ford recorded a video of himself along the lake’s shore near Hamilton, Ontario, where he revealed a baby-blue, billboard-sized sign that reads “Lake Ontario” in large white letters.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

Underneath, a subheading underscores Ford’s message about the name: “Now and Always.” The message is also repeated in French, Canada’s second official language.
Ford, who has made a habit of needling the US president, explained that the sign was erected to reaffirm the Great Lake’s name “in case President Trump — or anyone else — forgets”.
“Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in his social media video. “And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario.”
The White House did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
With Canada and the US embroiled in a spiralling trade war, Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that changed how the US federal government would refer to the body of water.
The order, however, drew pushback from allies and critics alike. Vermont Governor Phil Scott, a fellow Republican, called the move “petty and disappointing”, and several politicians urged Trump to return to the negotiating table, rather than antagonise Canada, a longtime ally.
Canada is ranked as one of the US’s top two trading partners, and as of 2024, it is the largest destination for US exports.
The trade tensions, however, have led to a popular backlash in Canada, with boycotts of US goods and bans in several provinces against US liquor.
Ford, a right-wing populist, has emerged as a vocal proponent of Canadian retaliatory actions. Since Trump took office for a second term in 2025, he has called for Canada to cede its sovereignty and become a US state, and has issued several waves of tariffs against the northern country.
Ford’s “Lake Ontario” sign marks the premier’s latest salvo in his ongoing feud with Trump.
Earlier this week, Ford escalated his attacks against Trump after trade negotiations between the two countries fell apart, resulting in US tariffs of 50 percent on $20bn worth of Canadian goods.
“He can kiss my a** as far as I’m concerned. We’re going to go at him full steam,” Ford said about Trump during a Monday interview on a Toronto radio show.
Trump fired back on his Truth Social platform by mocking Ford as “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive” compared with his late brother, the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
“Someone should get these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE,” Trump added.
Saturday’s billboard is not the first stunt Ford has undertaken to stand up against Trump, either. Some of those actions have had international consequences.
Last year, Ford’s government spent $75m on an anti-tariff advertisement featuring the voice of former US President Ronald Reagan, which aired in the US.
“Over the long run, such trade barriers hurt every American worker and consumer,” Reagan can be heard saying in the message.
The US and Canada were in the midst of trade negotiations at the time, and Trump cancelled the talks in protest against the advertisement. Some members of the Trump administration compared the advertising campaign with election interference, as the advertisements aired before 2025’s off-year races.
Ford ultimately pulled the advertisement from the airwaves in October, saying he had achieved his goal “to initiate a conversation” about “the impact of tariffs on workers and businesses”.
Since 2018, Ford has led Ontario as its provincial head of government. The province is considered the centre of Canada’s automotive manufacturing industry, and its factories are tightly integrated with US car manufacturers across the border.
A prominent conservative and longtime leader in Toronto, Ford formerly drew comparisons with Trump. His entry into provincial politics coincided with Trump’s first term as president.
Early on, some of Ford’s supporters rallied around the tagline “Make Ontario Great Again”, a play on Trump’s “Make America Great Again” campaign slogan. The phrase, in turn, had been popularised during Reagan’s 1980 run for president.
But Ford has rejected any comparisons with the US president, saying he and his family were involved in politics long before Trump.
