Doctors urge kids to get vaccinated ahead of school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:47:10 UTC
01:47:10 KST

With school beginning this week and COVID-19 and influenza activity at high levels, doctors at the Taiwan Immunization Vision and Strategy said children are at higher risk of infection and should get vaccinated as soon as a new program begins.
COVID-19 is still in the epidemic period, with weekly cases at a high level, while weekly flu cases in the past few weeks were at the highest level for the period in a decade, Centers for Disease Control (CDC) data showed.
Infection risks might increase as students return to school, the CDC said.
Photo: Lin Huei-chin, Taipei Times
Taiwan Immunization Vision and Strategy chairman Lee Ping-ing (李秉穎) said that young children are at high risk of severe flu complications, and with the recent high levels of flu and COVID-19, and school starting, children face a risk of contracting both.
The flu is not a common cold, he said, adding that in addition to pneumonia, children might also develop severe complications, including encephalitis, encephalopathy and myocarditis.
A US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report on flu-associated pediatric deaths in the US in the 2024-2025 flu season showed that among the documented clinical complications before death in children, 38 percent had pneumonia, while 18 percent had encephalopathy or encephalitis, the association said.
Children have a substantially higher risk of infection from outside the household than adults, but they are also the largest source of secondary transmission, often passing the disease to family members in the same household, it said, citing a study from Japan.
Taiwan Immunization Vision and Strategy executive member Huang Yu-cheng (黃玉成) said young children are often exposed to cluster infection risks at daycare centers, preschools or after-school care facilities.
The condition of children with the flu can deteriorate rapidly, so caregivers should seek immediate medical attention if warning signs of severe illness arise, including rapid breathing, altered consciousness, abnormal tiredness or clearly reduced activity levels, Huang said.
Some children might be afraid to get a vaccine shot, especially young children, so Taiwan last year introduced a nasal spray flu vaccine, he said, adding that the product is available for children and adolescents aged two through 17 years old and paid out of pocket.
The nasal spray flu vaccine is sprayed directly into the nasal cavity, inducing the nasal mucosa to produce antibodies for an immune response, Huang said.
It only takes a few seconds to provide protection, so it is a needle-free alternative for those who are unwilling to get traditional flu shots and will hopefully increase overall vaccine coverage rates, he said.
Parents should get their children vaccinated as soon as possible after the government-funded COVID-19 and flu vaccination program begins in October, Lee said.

KMT lawmaker says birthrate measures have failed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:40 UTC
01:46:40 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) lawmaker yesterday criticized the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) government over the nation’s declining population, calling it Taiwan’s top national security threat.
The National Development Council on Friday said that Taiwan’s population would fall below 20 million by 2045.
The prospect of a declining population is immediate and real, threatening Taiwan’s economy, finances, healthcare, social welfare and national security, KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said yesterday.
Photo: CNA
The decreasing workforce would come under increasing pressure to support the National Health Insurance program, pay taxes, provide people to defend the nation and care for a growing population of elderly people, Hsu said.
The DPP government is not truly aware of the pressures facing the younger generation, she said, citing real-estate prices, stagnant wages, surging commodity prices and low savings.
The Executive Yuan’s decision not to countersign the Taiwan Youth Development and Future Account Act (台灣兒少成長及未來帳戶條例) passed by the Legislative Yuan earlier this month is evidence that the DPP government is oblivious to the issue, she said.
President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration is calling on people to marry and have children, but fails to understand that doing so involves costs ranging from housing and childbirth to child-rearing, daycare and education, Hsu said, adding that education is an expense for more than two decades for most people.
Many couples spend every waking minute weighing decisions against the pressure of rent, mortgage, baby formula and daycare expenses, she said.
Lai has failed to fulfill campaign pledges to build more social housing, she said.
When the prospect of a stable life is constantly assaulted by fresh waves of anxiety, it is difficult to muster the courage to bring another life into this world, Hsu said.
KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said the DPP government over the past eight years has allocated nearly NT$600 billion (US$18.97 billion) to address the low birthrate, but has failed to reverse the trend.
Young adults cite high housing prices, the cost of raising children and an unwillingness to change their lifestyles as the top three reasons for not having children, Lee said, adding that their collective decision is bringing Taiwan closer to a population crisis.
The number of births in 2012 was 230,000, but fell to 108,000 last year and is expected to be below 100,000 this year, she said.
The government should convene a national affairs meeting on the birthrate issue, she said.
If the trend cannot be reversed, Taiwan risks going from a thriving and prosperous technological place to somewhere devoid of people, she added.

Taiwan in Time: The once-bustling temple atop 1,200 steps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Aug. 31 to Sept. 6
More than 3 million people visited Taipei’s Zhinan Temple (指南宮) in 1973, making it Taiwan’s second-most visited scenic area that year.
Built in 1891, the temple had been a tourist destination since the Japanese colonial period, when visitors had to initially take a ferry across the Jingmei River before climbing a winding trail up Houshan (猴山).
Photo courtesy of Academia Historica
Its popularity was reflected in popular media. The 1932 tune New Song of the Black Cat and Black Dog (新烏貓烏狗歌) depicted two lovers who prayed at the temple for their marriage. The man couldn’t afford to hire a sedan chair, so they made the arduous journey on foot. They later committed suicide after the man was unable to pay the bride price demanded by the woman’s family.
The 1959 movie Brother Wang and Brother Liu Tour Taiwan (王哥柳哥遊台灣) featured the titular duo huffing and puffing their way up the temple’s stairs on their first stop.
Although visitor numbers have declined from their historic peak, Zhinan Temple remains a destination for many, with the Maokong Gondola making a stop there. Its Lingxiao Hall, completed in 1966, was seriously damaged in a fire on Monday. Officials say the rest of the complex will remain open.
Photo courtesy of National Museum of Taiwan History via Open Museum
DISPUTED ORIGINS
The principal deity of Zhinan Temple is the Taoist immortal Lu Tung-pin (呂洞賓). According to the temple, sacred incense representing Lu Tung-pin’s spiritual presence was brought from China in 1882 by Wang Pin-lin (王斌林), who had been appointed magistrate of Tamsui County. The deity was initially housed in Wanhua District (萬華), but locals later invited it to Jingmei District (景美) during an epidemic. After the sickness passed, local gentry built a small thatched-roof shrine on Muzha District’s (木柵) Houshan in 1890 to honor the deity.
But this account is disputed. The National Taiwan University database of Qing officials lists Wang as a county deputy in Bangka (today’s Wanhua), rather than as Tamsui magistrate. Taiwan Daily News reports suggest that he was already in Taiwan by 1878.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
Examining Japanese-era sources, historian Paul Katz traces Zhinan Temple to a spirit-writing temple in Wanhua dedicated to Lu. After hearing of the deity’s powers, Jingmei residents had Wanhua artisans carve an identical statue and established their own temple. Worshippers from nearby Muzha later joined them, and helped establish Zhinan Temple in 1891.
Ethnologist Wu Tsung-ming (吳宗明) argues that Wang was already established on Houshan in the 1880s, where spirit writing may also have taken place. Wang’s son, Wang Yu-ching (王毓卿), later worked with worshippers from Jingmei and Muzha to establish Zhinan Temple and served on its first board.
The temple no longer offers spirit-writing services, having shifted its focus to Taoism, with Buddhist and Confucian characteristics.
At first, visitors had to cross the Jingmei River from Muzha to reach the temple. They could make the crossing on foot when the water was low, writes Hsu Chung-chieh (徐仲杰) in “The formation of the religious attraction of Muzha Zhinan Temple” (宗教景點木柵宮的形成), but taking a ferry was the safer option. Around 1900, as the temple’s popularity grew, Muzha District head Chang Te-ming (張德明) and eight others purchased local farmland and used the collected rent to fund a free ferry service.
A Taiwan Daily News article in 1909 attributed the temple’s popularity not only to the efficacy of its principal deity, but also to the cool mountain air and superb views of Taipei. Lu Tung-pin was said to cure illnesses and provide worshippers with dreams that predict the future.
EXPANDING FACILITIES
Photo courtesy of Lienyuan Lee
The journey to the temple from Muzha’s main street took 30 to 40 minutes, painter Kinichiro Ishikawa wrote in the Taiwan Daily News in 1926, adding that “visiting once was enough.” The “thousand stone steps” leading to the temple already existed by then, and sources show beggars waiting along the route for visitors, Hsu writes.
By the 1920s, visitors could take a train to Jingmei and continue to Muzha by bus or pushcart. The crowds persisted into the intensified Japanization period of the late 1930s, when extra Lunar New Year buses were reportedly required despite government promotion of State Shinto. A 1938 report showed 700,000 to 800,000 visitors per year.
The temple began large-scale renovations and expansion in 1920, a project that took seven years to complete. A temporary wooden bridge was built in 1928 for the opening ceremony, but it survived only a few years before being damaged by torrential rains. The steel Daonan Bridge (道南橋) was completed in 1934, with a ceremony held in October. Although it was conducted by Shinto priests per government policy, it still featured the temple’s deities crossing the river and other Taoist elements.
Visitors continued to use the ferry afterward, although ridership gradually declined.
The stone steps were rebuilt in 1936, with stone lanterns and benches added along the way. Palm and pine trees were planted on either side for shade. Tourist photographers and vendors selling food, drinks and worship supplies set up shop outside the temple.
The temple remained popular after the war. A 1955 report recorded tens of thousands of people visiting during Lunar New Year, prompting bus companies to add more than 100 extra trips to Muzha.
MOTORIZED ERA
Although a road for motorized vehicles was built to the temple in 1955, general Hsu Yung-chang (徐永昌) recalled still hiring a sedan chair to traverse the steps in 1956. The government restricted the number of vehicles during Lunar New Year, and a 1980 United Daily News report described people waiting up to four hours to catch the bus down the mountain.
The grandiose Lingxiao Hall was completed in 1966. The structure was featured in the 1969 Hollywood thriller The Chairman starring Gregory Peck, where it served as a stand-in for Mao Tse-tung’s (毛澤東) residence in Beijing.
That same year, an amusement park and zoo were added to the temple complex, greatly boosting visitor numbers. The park closed in the 1980s, and the temple saw a decline in visitors during the 1990s. Bus routes were reduced, making the remote temple even less accessible.
The idea of building a cable car up to the temple dates back to the Japanese era. A 1932 Taiwan Daily News article briefly pondered the feasibility, and plans were repeatedly floated through the 1950s and 1960s. The gondola finally became a reality in 2007, and the rise of Maokong as a tourist destination brought the temple renewed attention.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
When we recall the 1990s, we usually identify them as the time of great transitions, from authoritarianism to democracy, and the public’s shift to acknowledging a Taiwanese identity. But another transition occurred, one that we take for granted and hardly notice anymore. The 1980s opened with the massacre of members of the family of democracy activist Lin I-hsiung (林義雄). While Lin was in detention, on Feb. 28, 1980, persons still unknown broke into the Lin family home despite round-the-clock police surveillance. Lin’s mother and two of his three daughters were slain. His eldest daughter survived multiple stab wounds. The following year
During the Martial Law era, newspapers and magazines were strictly controlled by the government. But from 1985 to 1990 — a period that straddled the lifting of martial law in 1987 — a free monthly expat magazine emerged as one of the first published and edited by foreigners. It was also perhaps the first to express a uniquely local expatriate voice. Taiwan Grapevine’s articles were irreverent, politically incorrect and plagued by typos. Taiwan’s rivers are significantly cleaner today than they were a few decades ago. The country’s rapid industrialization left many waterways polluted by untreated factory discharge, domestic sewage and runoff from livestock operations. Since the 1990s, expansion of municipal sewerage infrastructure and stricter enforcement of environmental standards have turned the situation around. Integrating immigrants
I am writing regarding Dino Wei’s (魏思源) article “Introducing Indian migrant workers” (April 22) [https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/editorials/archives/2026/04/22/2003856012].
Taiwan has a serious labor shortage, and its aging and declining population means the nation would need immigrants, Wei wrote. I agree that Taiwan should not rely on only a few countries for migrant workers and that bringing in Indian workers gradually is a reasonable approach.
However, Taiwan should not only ask how many immigrants the economy needs, but also how many immigrants Taiwanese society can realistically integrate.
Taiwan already has large communities of people from the Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam. If Taiwan wants immigrants from these countries to stay and eventually become permanent residents and citizens, they should also be expected to become part of Taiwanese society.
The nation should learn from Canada, the US, the UK and other countries. Immigration is not bad per se, but it must be managed properly, especially its pace, scale and concentration.
When large numbers of people from the same country or cultural background become concentrated in particular communities, there is a risk of creating parallel societies, with people living, working and socializing within their own circles without becoming part of the larger Taiwanese society.
Immigrants should be encouraged and expected to learn Mandarin, Taiwanese or English and participate in Taiwanese society. They should be free to maintain their own languages, traditions and culture, but people in Taiwan must also maintain a shared public culture and national identity.
There should be reasonable exceptions when political loyalties and national security are concerned. If someone comes from a country that is an adversary of Taiwan, such as China, the nation may reasonably require them to choose where their political loyalty lies.
Those who deliberately refuse to integrate, reject Taiwanese law and social norms, or actively seek to impose or replace Taiwanese culture, institutions or religious traditions, should not — regardless of their country of origin — automatically receive permanent residency or citizenship.
However, there are legal, cultural and social barriers in Taiwan that could make it difficult for immigrants to become fully accepted as Taiwanese. If Taiwan expects immigrants to integrate, it should also give them a realistic and equal opportunity to become Taiwanese once they have demonstrated genuine integration.
Taiwan should also consider whether immigrants who have lived in Taiwan, contributed to society, learned the language and genuinely made Taiwan their home should be able to retain their original citizenship when they become Taiwanese citizens. Taiwanese citizens and people of Taiwanese descent can have dual citizenship, so the government should seriously consider whether it could give immigrants who meet the same standards of integration the same opportunity.
Integration is primarily the responsibility of immigrants. They must demonstrate genuine effort to become part of Taiwan, but the nation must also reward that effort by accepting those who do. Taiwan needs immigrants, but immigration should not simply increase the number of people living and working in Taiwan. It should bring new people into Taiwanese society who can eventually say: “Taiwan is my home. I am Taiwanese.”
Paul Garrelfs
Toronto, Ontario,
Canada

The women of the spectral world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:33 UTC
01:46:33 KST

These past few weeks, I have not aired my laundry in public. Literally. This is not the result of some domestic crisis, but due to my recent induction to Ghost Month etiquette. That also means we have stayed away from walking near bodies of water, kept a safe distance from walls and provided a snack table for wandering spirits.
It is always interesting to learn how history, the environment and geography shape traditions and belief systems of cultures. Something that is always noticeable across geographies is how female ghosts play center stage in that realm. It is probably one of those rare arenas which is not a sole male bastion and where they are not edged off the playing field for being women. It is quite the opposite: They have managed to scare the hell out of people and keep society at large in line. Or is that really the case?
The “monstrous female” as per some theorists of cultural anthropology, is how horror and folklore is created around a female figure. They carry serious emotional baggage. Where male ghosts thrive on power, greed and lust, their female counterparts are dealing with much of what their human versions battle with: heartbreak, disenfranchisement and grief.
I am only beginning to learn about the haunting, but beautiful ladies in local folklore. I have heard of the Guniang (姑娘), the unwed female ghost; the Yingling (嬰靈), spirits of aborted or miscarried fetuses; and the Na Tao Ji (林投姊, or “screw pine tree sister”), a widow who was tricked by her Chinese lover. The woman in red or little girl in red are often mentioned in urban legends. These common themes extend to many other cultures.
The Onryo, from the Japanese spirit world, is a bitter, vengeful spirit in the aftermath of a tragic, unrequited love. The Yurei wreaks havoc due to a bad past and being jilted by a lover.
In Korean folklore, Cheonyeo gwisin or malmyeong are young unmarried women who died without playing their dutiful roles in society.
In Malaysia, the Pontianik is the vengeful spirit of a woman that died during childbirth.
And of course, the woman in white, weeping for her children or husband, is present in almost all cultures with different names — La Llorona from Mexico might be more familiar due to the Conjuring franchise.
The list of woes seemingly traverses the whole life cycle of a woman, from birth, to adolescence, love, marriage, childbirth or the lack of it, or grieving a family or a life that could have been, but was not.
India, with its diverse 4,635 social, ethnic and tribal groups, 121 spoken languages and more than 19,500 raw spoken dialects, has its fair share of female ghosts representing various social milieus and their realities.
The Churail is a woman who died during childbirth or due to family neglect. She lives in a tree, usually a Banyan or Peepal tree, and has feet turned the other way.
There are many seductresses on the prowl as well. Mohini, Yakshini or Dayan are on the lookout for men to entice and kill.
The male ghosts have rather elementary goals and are satiated by chopping off heads (Skandakata), hunting for fish (Mechho bhoot) or the pursuit of wealth (Jakha/Yaksha)
This might sound like an oversimplification of centuries of evolution that have shaped what we know of the spiritual world, but something to consider is that it was shaped by its participants, society, the men and women living in it.
Broadly speaking, the spectral world can be divided between ghosts that are meant to be an instrument of control or to keep society in check — about morals or for protection (do not swim on a moonless night, do not walk alone or listen to your elders) — and those that, as sociologist Avery Gordon put it, return because they were repressed. If this is true, then the quantum of female spirits just shows that they have more of an axe to grind.
For centuries, society has been conditioned into believing that loud women, bold women and women who choose love over duty, pleasure over sacrifice or freedom over family meet a horrible fate, in this life and the next.
Folklorists use the term “Deviant femme,” but Gordon said that “Feminist hauntology is a social phenomenon where the repressed, violent histories of a society refuse to stay buried.” And they find a voice through stories, lores, legends and superstitions.
What I love about Ghost month is that, at least to a third dispassionate eye, it seems to be neither about male or female ghosts: It is about honoring and respecting those, known and unknown, from another realm who are visiting and passing by. It makes it feel like an aunt dropping by, something familiar and generous, as opposed to something to be scared of.
In India, as part of the lunar calendar, much like the ghost month, we have a month of shraadh or pitru paksha which literally means “fortnight of the ancestors,” during which we, too, worship and honor those who are no longer with us.
This is another thing that turns out to be common between my homeland and the land that has embraced me and made me feel like I am home. And this visit is more than pleasant.
Richa S Mukherjee is a former journalist and author based in Taiwan.

What can you do with a simple roll of tape? The answer goes far beyond holding things together. Colorful, patterned, and surprisingly versatile paper tape has found its way into cards, journals, and even art projects. Interestingly, its story begins not in craft shops, but in a very different, industrial __1__.
In the 1920s, when two-toned cars were all the rage, workers struggled with their paint jobs. They __2__ what they had: newspaper or butcher paper, along with strong glue or adhesive tape. However, peeling the paper often __3__ fresh paint, forcing them to repair the damaged areas at extra cost. An employee named Richard Drew from 3M, then a sandpaper manufacturer, took note of this issue and set out to find a solution. He __4__ with various materials and eventually invented “masking tape.” This kind of tape features a crepe paper backing and a gentler adhesive, allowing it to stay in place during painting yet be removed without damaging the __5__.
Decades later, this invention took an unexpected turn in Japan. Kamoi Kakoshi, once known for making industrial masking tape, was __6__ by three paper tape lovers. They had used the company’s masking tape in craft books and suggested that it produce colorful tapes for handicrafts. The company took on the challenge and managed to __7__ practical masking tape into something artistic. This new masking tape was thin, slightly transparent, and made of Japanese washi paper, a traditional and durable material crafted from natural fiber. For the first time, tape was used not just to help things __8__ but also for decoration.

It is __9__ for an industrial product to develop into a cultural phenomenon. The evolution of paper tape shows that the line between a __10__ tool and an artistic medium is thinner than we think. 你可以拿單純的一捲膠帶來做什麼？答案遠遠不只是把東西固定在一起。色彩繽紛、帶有圖案，且意外多用途的紙膠帶已融入禮物卡、日記，甚至是藝術作品中。有趣的是，其故事不是從手工藝品店展開，而是始於非常不一樣的工業環境。
1920 年代，雙色車風靡一時，工人在進行噴漆作業時感到吃力。他們將就使用手邊的物品：報紙或屠夫紙，以及強力膠或膠帶。然而，撕除紙張常常會一併撕掉剛上好的漆，迫使工人要花額外的成本來修補受損的區域。3M 公司（當時為砂紙製造業者）一位名為理查德魯的員工注意到這個問題，便著手找解決辦法。他試驗多種材料，最終發明了「遮蔽膠帶」。這種膠帶的特色是皺紋紙基底和黏性較低的黏著劑，能在上漆時保持在固定位置，卻又不會毀損表面。
數十年後，這項發明在日本有了意想不到的轉變。三名紙膠帶愛好者接洽了「鴨井加工紙」，該公司曾因製造工業用遮蔽膠帶而聞名。他們之前曾在手工書上用了該公司的遮蔽膠帶，並建議其生產用於手工藝的繽紛膠帶。該公司接受了挑戰，成功將實用的遮蔽膠帶轉變為有藝術感的物品。這款新的遮蔽膠帶很薄、有點透明，且是由日本的和紙製成，和紙是用天然纖維製成的傳統、耐用材料。膠帶第一次不只是幫忙黏東西，還用於裝飾。
工業產品發展成文化現象很是罕見。紙膠帶的發展顯示，實用工具與藝術媒介之間的分界線比我們想的還細。當我們透過想像力來看，即使是簡單的一捲膠帶所能做的也不僅是把東西黏在一起而已。

Ivy learned the traditional craft from her mother.

這位藝術家用極大的耐心精心製作每一件作品。

Dubai chocolates are all the rage right now.

Peggy took note of her brother’s unusual behavior and decided to ask him about it.
佩姬注意到弟弟的不尋常行為，並決定問他怎麼回事。

The weather took a sudden turn as the rain hit.
雨彈來襲，天氣驟變。

The doctor suggested that the injured athlete (should) rest for at least one year.

Unknown

Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC) plans to gradually color-code platform signage, departure screens and information boards -- blue for northbound and green for southbound -- starting at the new Tainan Station, the company said yesterday.
The new underground Tainan Station -- which could open in mid-October pending safety inspections -- is already outfitted with the color-coded wayfinding system, making it the first station to feature the new design, the company said.
TRC disclosed the plan following a Ministry of Transportation and Communications media tour of the station on Friday.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Under the updated system, northbound (clockwise) routes are designated in blue, whereas southbound (counterclockwise) routes are in green. The design mirrors the layout used at Taiwan High Speed Rail stations.
The company noted that in addition to the color-coded system, platform nameboards at the new underground Tainan Station feature a minimalist layout displaying the station name (in Chinese, English, Japanese and Korean) and adjacent stops to enhance readability.
In contrast, traditional station boards also feature the company logo, photos of local attractions and distances between adjacent stops, in addition to station names in Chinese and English.
TRC said it will gradually allocate funds to upgrade the wayfinding system across its network, though it did not provide a specific timeline.

Du Toit crosses 100 Tests for Springboks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:21 UTC
01:46:21 KST

When Pieter-Steph du Toit came into the orbit of Rassie Erasmus in 2018, the new South Africa coach was not impressed.
Du Toit had already been a Springbok for five years and collected one domestic player of the year award, but Erasmus had never met or worked with him.
His take on Du Toit was someone who missed or slipped off too many tackles and ran too upright as a ball-carrier. Erasmus took Du Toit’s nonchalance as uncaring. At best, Erasmus thought Du Toit had utility value on the bench.
Photo: AP
“I have never been as wrong about a player as I was with Pieter-Steph, and I have never been as pleased to be so wrong,” Erasmus said in an interview with SA Rugby.
Over the weekend, Du Toit became the 11th player with 100 Tests for the Springboks and the sixth on Erasmus’ watch as coach or director.
Erasmus was appointed in 2018 to resurrect South Africa after two humbling years. He wanted players who could make the Springboks respected and revered again, and it took only two training sessions for him to realize Du Toit was one of them.
Erasmus was gratified by Du Toit’s commitment to the jersey, knowledge of the game, contributions, enthusiasm to learn and be challenged. He was first on, last off. He had to be forced to take a day off. Married to that were sharp instincts on the field, a willingness for dirty work, ability to get over the gainline and disrupt attacks with tackles that punished carriers.
The clincher for the coach was in September 2018, a year after a 57-0 hiding from New Zealand in Auckland, they won in New Zealand for the first time in nine years. Du Toit made 24 tackles and cameras caught him in tears after the game.
Now, Erasmus could not drop him. His “Bomb Squad” packed with reserve forwards might replace captain Siya Kolisi before Du Toit, if at all. Du Toit’s engine is legendary. He rarely plays less than the full 80 minutes in a test.
Du Toit wanted to be a great Springbok from a young age. He grew up on tales and mementos of his grandfather, Piet du Toit, nicknamed “Spiere,” or “Muscles” in Afrikaans. Piet anchored the Springboks scrum in the successful home series against the 1960 All Blacks and on the 1960-1961 Grand Slam tour of the home nations.
Du Toit was raised on the vineyard and olive groves bought by Piet in the 1950s and still farmed by the family, an hour outside of Cape Town.
His journey to greatness has been far from plain sailing.
He would have got to 100 tests much earlier but for a cracked sternum, lots of shoulder injuries and two reconstructed ACLs, the second for which he got a hamstring tendon from his father to hasten recuperation in time for the 2015 Rugby World Cup in England.
His World Cup debut was the infamous loss to Japan, the Miracle of Brighton. Du Toit was part of the fallout for being played out of position.
His worst injury was almost career-ending. A thigh hematoma in February 2020 became unbearably painful and he underwent emergency surgery. He had acute compartment syndrome, a dangerous buildup of pressure inside muscles.
The doctors’ cut in his thigh was 40cm long. Later, when nerves were not responding, leg amputation was considered. Losing 10kg helped to ease a fourth operation to close the wound.
At the time, Du Toit was a new World Cup champion and world player of the year.
In the 2019 final win over England, he made 20 tackles and asked forwards coach Matt Proudfoot afterward what he could improve.
“He’s a no-nonsense guy who doesn’t seek validation,” Proudfoot said. “He just wants to know what he’s got to do. He doesn’t say much but the group listens. He just puts it out there. Being a Springbok matters to him.”
Du Toit easily admits he is not a talker.
“I’m a strong believer in actions speak louder than words,” he said. “The way you perform on the field or the way you live your life must tell your story, ‘Okay, these are the morals of this guy.’ And if you can do that, nothing has to be said.”
The one time he did speak up was captured on video and proved inspirational.
South Africa was trailing England 12-6 at halftime in the 2023 World Cup semi-finals in Paris. Erasmus left the changing room which fell unnaturally quiet. Du Toit stood up and asked his teammates if they were scared or wanted to fight, laced with obscenities.
When the speech appeared in “Chasing the Sun 2,” documenting South Africa’s run to the title, Du Toit was worried his foul language might make kids think he was not a good role model.
In the final against New Zealand, Du Toit made a staggering 28 tackles without a miss and was named the player of the match.
Then-Springboks coach Jacques Nienaber joked, “If there’s a white plastic bag that blows over the pitch, he’d probably chase that down as well.”

Ultra cyclist James MacDonald’s previous feats often involved soul-destroying hours lapping velodromes but today, the intrepid Scot sets out on a much more scenic record attempt.
The Google software engineer plans to ride five of the toughest one-day races in professional cycling — back-to-back in four days — starting with the iconic 258km Paris-Roubaix.
He would then tackle the fabled cobbles of the 278km Tour of Flanders, followed by the Liege-Bastogne-Liege and Il Lombardia before finishing on Wednesday with the 298km Milan-San Remo.
MacDonald plans to ride a cumulative 1,349km across France, Belgium and Italy — with his only rest coming during transfers between the different routes in the support vehicle.
“There’s a big difference going from A to B instead of going round in circles,” the 55-year-old MacDonald, whose bid to set a new indoor record for 100 miles (160.9km) was wrecked by illness at the London velodrome two years ago, said in an interview.
Riding the five cycling “Monuments” back-to-back has never been officially done before so his pace, including transfer times, would set a benchmark for future challengers.
MacDonald has competed in endurance cycling events for more than 20 years. He once completed the 3,089 mile (4,971.3km) Race Across America as a solo rider in 2016, set the fastest recorded return time between John O’ Groats and Land’s End in 2017, and broke the indoor 100km record in 2021.
Last year, as a warm-up for his five monuments challenge, he added his third Guinness record for taking the shortest time to ride the 625km between Scotland’s most widely separated points — Mull of Galloway to John O’ Groats.
“Of all the challenges I have taken on, this feels like the one I have been building toward,” MacDonald, who has spent two years planning the ride working with the World Ultra Cycling Association, said.
“The Monuments are the defining one-day races in professional cycling, and nobody has attempted all five back-to-back in this format before. With the clock running continuously, every decision will matter, from how hard I push, when I sleep and how quickly the team can move me between routes.”
The longest transfer would be from Liege down to Bergamo for Il Lombardia and one strict condition from the association is that a tracker ensures no speeding on the motorized sections.
“Those 10 hours off the bike [between Liege and Bergamo] will be tough, especially after 700km on the bike, that might feel awful,” MacDonald said.
MacDonald has never ridden any of the five routes, but says the weather forecast in France and Belgium could make it feel more like Scotland, and that riding the Tour of Flanders at night could be disorientating.
But the roll down to the Mediterranean on the Ligurian Riviera is something to look forward to.
“The pacing plan is that I’ll hit the coast at sunrise. The profile for San Remo is basically uphill and then it drops off a cliff as you get toward the Mediterranean.”
Despite riding in Europe’s culinary hot spots, MacDonald does not have time to indulge and is following the advice of his nutritionists in his support team, led by challenge manager Matt Jones of Perpetual Sports Consulting.
“It’s going to be pretty systematic for me,” he said. “Energy gels, brioche buns, croissants, energy powders, chocolate milk. And lots of coffee.”

China, Russia, Iran leaders to meet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) are expected tomorrow in Kyrgyzstan for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran’s and India’s leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West. Around a dozen heads of states would head to the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West. It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran would be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Photo: Reuters
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.
Putin is expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran — among the most sanctioned states in the world — have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran. Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in the past few years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership. On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 “dialogue partners,” including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states.”
However, Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation,” referring to US-Chinese tensions.
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are amid real wars — the Ukraine and Iran conflicts — or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation and maritime transport, aiming to cripple the Iranian regime.
Washington also threatened Iran’s allies with sanctions. China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it would “firmly defend” its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure. However, Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces “economic difficulties.”
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023. Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, said that Tehran “believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions.”
However, concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as “in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties.”
While the bloc claims to represent about 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia — a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia — while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.

Audit shows Taipei child protection system lapses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:11 UTC
01:46:11 KST

Nearly 20 percent of reports to Taipei’s child protection system were deemed invalid, while as of the end of August last year, 303 cases involving alleged violations of the law had passed the legal deadlines for investigation and penalties, the National Audit Office said in a report.
The reports, which are processed by the Taipei Social Welfare Department’s Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault Prevention Center, increased from 9,217 in 2023 to 12,259 last year, with more than 90 percent filed by “mandatory reporters” each year, it said.
Mandatory reporters — teachers, doctors, social workers, police, childcare staff and others — are required to report possible breaches of the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act (兒童及少年福利與權益保障法) within 24 hours.
Photo: CNA
While department data show that attendance at training sessions for mandatory reporters has been high — with annual check-ins at classes from 2023 to last year ranging from 15,000 to more than 25,000 — the number of invalid reports submitted has increased each year and account for nearly 20 percent, it said.
The instances of duplicate reports, out-of-date cases, cases unrelated to child protection and reports with insufficient information are concerning, it said.
Reporting accuracy and mandatory reporters’ ability to identify cases had not clearly improved, despite the training, the audit said, adding that the situation could affect resource allocation and case-handling efficiency.
New learning technologies should have been introduced to develop a decisionmaking support model based on big data analysis and case triage guidelines, it said, citing the second phase of the Strengthening the Social Safety Net Program.
However, the department still bases its case assessments and assignments primarily on manual judgements, it said.
Given the increasing caseload, frontline personnel might face too great a burden to conduct consistent and efficient case judgements, the National Audit Office said.
Regarding case processing time, statutory deadlines are classified — depending on urgency and case type — as within four days, within 30 days, or within four months with a one-month extension allowed when necessary, the office said.
However, the department received 2,218 reports of contraventions of the act from 2023 to the end of June last year, with 365 still pending at the end of August last year — 62 waiting on court rulings and 303 overdue for other reasons, such as delays in obtaining reports from other agencies, or delays in collecting evidence or soliciting statements, it said.
As of August last year, there were six overdue cases from 2023 and 103 from 2024, showing that the department must improve its reporting quality, case assessment mechanisms and case processing speed, the office said.
The department yesterday said that the center would continue to conduct training in collaboration with reporting units to improve the ability of mandatory reporters to assess and identify child-protection incidents.
The department would introduce tools to help screen cases in line with the central government’s policy to boost screening efficiency and reduce the burden on frontline child protection personnel, it said.
As of the end of last year, case backlogs from 2023 and 2024 were reduced to four and 52 respectively, the department said, adding that it would continue to review and track the progress.

Reports of US funding cuts to Kurdish armed forces raises concerns over regional stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:24:22 UTC
01:24:22 KST

The Trump administration is planning to cut funding to the Peshmerga, the armed forces of the Kurdistan Regional Government, according to a BBC report that called the Peshmerga "a key Middle East ally that helped the US defeat the Islamic State group (IS) and is now facing punishing attacks from Iran, according to four sources familiar with the matter."
Kurdish media Rudaw said Washington had not informed the Peshmerga of a plan to cut funding.
Discussions and concerns about the US reducing funding for the Peshmerga have been key issues for years. The Peshmerga have played a key role over the years fighting ISIS and securing the autonomous Kurdistan Region. However, efforts to reform them have not proceeded as planned. In addition, the US is withdrawing from Iraq on September 30.
A bit of history helps explain the issues involved.
The Kurdish Peshmerga have been an important military force in the Middle East in the last decade. The Peshmerga date back to the Kurdish national movement of the twentieth century. Following the establishment of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War, the Peshmerga became the region's official security force. However, the force remained divided between the two dominant Kurdish political parties: the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), whose military formation became known as Division (or Unit) 80, and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), whose forces were organized as Division (or Unit) 70. This division complicated command and control despite cooperation against common threats.
US expands military assistance after Kurdish forces halts ISIS advance
The rise of ISIS in 2014 highlighted both the strengths and challenges facing the Peshmerga. Kurdish forces played a decisive role in halting ISIS's advance, defending Erbil, protecting displaced civilians, and later participating in the campaigns to liberate Sinjar, Kirkuk, and areas surrounding Mosul.
Their battlefield performance led the United States and the Global Coalition to significantly expand military assistance, training, and equipment programs. There had been an effort to reform the forces before 2014. The concept was to move them away from party affiliation toward a neutral Peshmerga ministry. The ISIS war and the 2017 Kurdistan Independence referendum delayed this effort.
A central component of that effort by the international community to support the Peshmerga has been the Kurdistan Training Coordination Center (KTCC) in Erbil. Established by coalition partners during Operation Inherent Resolve, the KTCC has coordinated multinational training programs, standardized instruction, and helped professionalize Kurdish units. Coalition members have trained thousands of Peshmerga soldiers in infantry tactics, staff planning, leadership, logistics, and specialized military skills while also advising the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs on broader institutional reform.
I witnessed this firsthand on visits to the region. The training was paying off. The Peshmerga Ministry was trying to modernize.
However, the region faces many crises. Baghdad has sought to weaken the region economically. There have been threats from Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Turkey has also operated in areas near the border. The KDP and PUK can’t get along in the regional parliament. Everything is on hold due to local political squabbles. The result is that international support is sometimes either taken for granted or not leveraged to its full potential.
BBC wrote that “the US Department of Defense has told leaders of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region in recent meetings that the administration is not planning to renew an expiring agreement that provides security assistance to the Peshmerga, the Kurdish security force.”
Funding cut may embolden Iran
The report notes that “Kurdish officials fear the funding cut would create a power vacuum and embolden Iran, which has fired hundreds of missiles and drones into Iraqi Kurdistan since US President Donald Trump started the war with Tehran.” Yerevan Saeed, the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, told the BBC that "the US would be cutting off the Kurds, who shed so much blood to help the Americans achieve their goals in Iraq and the wider Middle East…This is going to be a big win for Iran, China, and Russia if the Kurds are left so exposed."
The report added that the Peshmerga has around 180,000 troops in Iraqi Kurdistan and they “received $61m (£45m) in the fiscal year 2026 for weapons, military training and stipends through the Pentagon's counter-IS program.”
For such a large force, this isn’t a lot of funds. However, the US is dealing with many issues in the region. It is trying to deal with Gaza and Lebanon and the war with Iran.
BBC notes that “the Pentagon signed the initial memorandum of understanding giving military assistance to the Peshmerga in 2016 and renewed it in 2022. A final decision on security engagement between the US and Kurdistan is still being reviewed, according to one source familiar with the Pentagon's thinking. The US is considering ways to maintain some security support in both Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan after the troop withdrawal, the sources said.”
According to Kurdish media outlet Rudaw, “Washington has not officially informed the Kurdistan Region's Peshmerga ministry of plans to halt financial assistance as a security agreement nears expiry, three informed sources told Rudaw on Saturday, after the BBC reported that the United States had told Erbil the deal would not be renewed.” The report noted that "regarding the termination of the aid, the US has told the Ministry of Peshmerga nothing officially," a senior ministry official told Rudaw’s Soran Hussein on Saturday.

Jerusalem's L3 opens after years of delays, turning one light rail line into a network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:24:15 UTC
01:24:15 KST

Living in central Jerusalem can be defined by a few key characteristics: the shuk, the noise, and, of course, the light rail.
Nearly a full year after we here at The Jerusalem Post bemoaned the temporary loss of the Haturim station, the payoff has arrived, and the L3 segment – the first section to open as part of the broader Green Line project and currently highlighted in yellow – opened to the public this week, running from Haturim to the Malha Mall.
The city went all in on the yellow branding, with balloon arches at every station, yellow signs, and lemon-flavored popsicles marking the grand opening.
The line’s opening was headlined by a who’s who of the Jerusalem infrastructure world, and was celebrated by Transportation Minister Miri Regev, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion, and Cfir CEO Oren Cohen.
The L3 route spans seven kilometers, running from Haturim station west through the Central Bus Station and the Navon rail station, before heading south to the Knesset and Hebrew University’s Givat Ram campus. It then stops at Teddy Stadium and Pais Arena before ending near the Malha Mall and the expanding Gav Yam tech park. The segment adds 12 stations to the network alongside the existing Haturim interchange and the Central Bus Station/Navon hub.
What matters most is that for the first time, Jerusalemites can transfer from one light rail line to another, and residents finally get to see what all that construction and noise has been about.
“It’s very reliable and convenient, and I don’t have to worry about missing my bus because, you know, it actually comes on time,” one passenger said after the launch. “Getting to Malha is a breeze now.”
Red Line recently expanded
The Red Line, the city’s first light rail corridor, has operated for 15 years, with recent expansions creating a vital link between Neve Yaakov and Hadassah Ein Kerem, carrying 200,000 riders daily.
However, as is common for public transport projects worldwide, the launch faced severe delays. Globes reported that the Green Line’s L3 phase opened 10 years later than planned, whereas earlier projections had envisioned the entire line being fully completed by 2025.
The delays over the past few years were compounded by the rounds of fighting with Iran, which disrupted construction and pushed the project’s timeline further.
The venture was initially approved by City Council in 2016, with tenders issued soon afterward, and construction has stretched across nearly a decade. The Green Line is also following a pattern familiar to residents: the Red Line’s extensions, initially slated for completion in 2023, were repeatedly pushed back before opening.
For residents along the route, the wait has meant years of construction, detours, and disrupted access to streets and businesses in areas including Givat Mordechai, Pat, and Jaffa Road.
But whether the delays were over a decade or just one year, the L3 is finally here, and Israel’s officials have been eager to frame the Green Line as a turning point for Jerusalem, even if some passengers found themselves decidedly underwhelmed.
“It smells like plastic which was just poured into a mold,” one passenger stated. “Also, it’s somehow already dirty, and I’m not surprised.”
For Mayor Moshe Lion, the opening marks a transformation in the city’s public transit landscape. “Jerusalem is moving from a city that has a light rail to a city with a light rail network,” he said, noting that the L3 marks the first step toward a fully interconnected transit grid.
“Together with the expanding park-and-ride facilities, this will soon become the city’s transportation backbone, transform its appearance and quality of life, connect neighborhoods, employment centers, and major institutions, and enable drivers to leave their private vehicles at home, and thus reduce traffic congestion and air pollution. L3 is not the finish line. The network will expand with additional lines, connect more and more parts of Jerusalem, and turn it into an accessible and advanced city like capitals and major cities around the world.”
Transportation Minister Miri Regev, who toured the line with Lion ahead of its opening, has similarly cast the project as part of a broader transportation revolution in the capital.
“Jerusalem continues to lead Israel’s public transport revolution and to demonstrate the direction in which we are taking transport in the major metropolitan areas: fast, efficient, interconnected, and accessible mass transit networks,” Regev said.
“The opening of the L3 line is a big step in our vision of connecting Israel and enabling all of its residents to reach their destinations quickly, comfortably, and safely.”
The next milestone is slated for December, when the L4 segment is set to link the Central Bus Station to Gilo in the south, the city’s largest neighborhood. This next phase will help more than 100,000 residents who are underserved by the light rail.
From there, the Green Line is expected to extend north toward Hebrew University’s Mount Scopus campus, scheduled to open by June 2027, running through French Hill and connecting the university’s two campuses by rail, which has been discussed by planners long before ground was even broken.
Looking to the future, the city has already begun construction on the Blue Line, set to run 24 km. from Ramot in the north to Gilo in the south, with 40 new stations.
However, that phase of the light rail isn’t projected to launch before 2029 or 2030, and the construction will bring several more years of the same street-level disruption residents just lived through with the Green Line.
Hopefully, the city will feel the same relief when that line opens as well.
Last week’s launch highlights Jerusalem’s success with surface light rail, contrasting with the far more complex and costly engineering of Tel Aviv’s $50 billion heavy underground metro system, which remains years away from completion.
While construction formally began with a cornerstone ceremony in December 2025, the tenders for the actual tunneling work are only now moving through pre-qualification, with operations not projected before the early-to-mid 2030s.
Bragging rights are great, but the stakes go further.
The light rail could eventually carry as many as 400,000 riders a day, easing a traffic problem that has only worsened, as Israel continues to suffer from some of the worst traffic congestion in the OECD.
For a city like Jerusalem, a genuine rail network does change who can live where and still remain connected to the heart of the city.
“Knowing that I don’t have to live right in the center of the city to benefit from the accessible transport will make living in Jerusalem easier in the long-term,” another passenger said.
One week in, it’s like the new stations have been with us all along, as commuters have already gotten used to checking updated schedules. The balloon arches have come down, but the trains keep on running.
For a city that has waited the better part of a decade for this moment, the milestone wasn’t really the ribbon-cutting, but the ordinariness of a new option simply existing.
The next test comes in December, when the line pushes farther south to Gilo. For now, Jerusalem has what it didn’t have a week ago: a network, not just a line.

Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:20:00 UTC
01:20:00 KST

Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
August 29, 2026
Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump.
In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department.
The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity."
The "Trump Route" is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project.
Experts have said construction of the "Trump Route" fits Washington's strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran.
Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia
Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia.
In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country's largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.
An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia's second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia's state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company.
"Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank," said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia.
Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer
While Armenia's government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country's infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks.
Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov's most vocal critics in parliament. He said it's alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years.
Manukyan's faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the "Trump Route" as a disguised "extraterritorial corridor" and the "greatest threat" to Armenia's security.
Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips.
His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff.
In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump's MAGA movement over the course of a year.
'Compromise' between Moscow and Washington?
Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov's appointment to head the fund.
The first is political. Appointing an American with Russian roots could be "a subtle gesture by Washington aimed at easing Moscow's fierce criticism of the project," he told DW.
The second, however, is pragmatic. "Perhaps Russia has nothing to do with it at all. Sokolov may simply have been chosen because he has a deep understanding of the business environment in the former Soviet Union — and because he knows Armenia and how its government works," said Poghosyan.
At the same time, the sheer scale of the investment and the financier's Russian roots are fueling speculation in Armenia. Social media users in the country are debating whether Sokolov, who was born in St. Petersburg, could be a secret "compromise figure" between Moscow and Washington. Supporters of the theory point to the ease with which US companies have acquired formerly Russian assets subject to Western sanctions.
Other observers have refuted the idea, noting that Sokolov has publicly and sharply criticized the Russian government and its war against Ukraine. The funds provided by the US State Department, running through 2036, are seen as flagging Washington's long-term strategic intentions in the region. During his visit to Yerevan, Aryeh Lightstone told Armenian news outlet CivilNet that the more than $200 million in initial funding could be viewed as a starting point for future investments.
Aram Sargsyan, head of the Republican Party of Armenia and an ally of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also rejects the idea that Sokolov is a "compromise figure" for Moscow. He emphasized the practical value of Sokolov's background, seeing it as an opportunity rather than a cause for concern.
"Sokolov has significant business contacts, understands the Russian mentality perfectly, speaks the language and knows how to work with relevant Russian institutions," he said.
This article was originally written in Russian.

RSS chief’s visit to US denounced as ‘goodwill tour’ for Hindu nationalism
Activists say Hindu nationalists have sought to mask far-right politics through broad appeals to the Indian diaspora.
An event in New York City featuring a prominent Hindu nationalist is being promoted as an invitation to send a positive message that “the world is one family”.
But an array of faith groups, advocacy organisations and unprivileged-caste organisations say they are not convinced. They fear Saturday’s rally, held at Madison Square Garden, is instead a high-profile effort to whitewash a record of discrimination and violence.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Oneness or Hindu supremacy? RSS chief Bhagwat’s secretive New York hosts
- list 2 of 3What is Hindutva, and what are the roots of this political movement?
- list 3 of 3Why India’s RSS is lobbying the West amid attacks on minorities at home
At issue is the Universal Oneness Celebration, hosted by the American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, a nonprofit that purports to advance “greater peace and harmony”.
One of its keynote speakers, however, will be Mohan Bhagwat, the leader of the Hindu paramilitary organisation Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). His organisation has been accused of embracing discriminatory policies and stoking violence against minorities, including India’s Muslim, Christian and Sikh populations.
Protests are expected outside Madison Square Garden to denounce Bhagwat’s appearance.
“This is a movement that has normalised mob violence against Muslims, attacks on Muslim men in relationships with Hindu women and the bulldozing of Muslim homes,” said Safa Ahmed, a Muslim community organiser in North Carolina who has travelled to New York to join the protests.
She told Al Jazeera she is sceptical about the event organisers’ claims about embracing the world as “one family”.
“They may speak about unity, but it’s in stark contrast with the bloody reality faced by minorities in India,” she said.
Overseas outreach
Advocates say that Hindu nationalist groups are working to expand their influence in the United States, where roughly 2.5 million Hindus live.
To do that, they have utilised a variety of appeals to soften the image of the RSS, such as celebrations of Hindu culture and campaigns to highlight anti-Hindu discrimination.
Sravya Tadepalli, the deputy executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, sees Saturday’s rally as part of that trend. Her group opposes the event.
“This is kind of a goodwill tour to improve the public image of the RSS, which is a fascist paramilitary organisation that has engaged in decades of communal violence against religious minorities in South Asia,” Tadepalli told Al Jazeera.
“The organisations behind this have pitched it as a broad appeal to Hindu history with an emphasis on inclusivity when, in reality, the RSS advocates for the exact opposite.”
Critics have pointed out, however, that Hindu nationalists have also sought to cultivate links with the global far-right, emphasising a shared belief in the purported threats posed by Islam and secular elites.
The RSS is widely considered the ideological parent of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has ruled India since 2014 and sought to remake the country along Hindu nationalist lines.
In remarks to the 2024 National Conservatism Conference in Washington, DC, BJP Vice President Ram Madhav said that conservatives in the West should view India as an example of how to defeat what he called the “left, liberal, Marxist, radical Islamist cabal”.
The Modi model
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who entered politics as an RSS cadre before becoming the head of the BJP, has championed Hindu nationalism throughout his leadership.
Like Bhagwat, he has also taken his message on the road, to speak to overseas supporters in the US.
In September 2019, for instance, the prime minister addressed a crowd of 50,000 at a “Howdy, Modi!” rally in the state of Texas.
The event underscored Modi’s appeal among Indians living abroad and was one of the largest such events in US history. US President Donald Trump, another far-right leader, even joined Modi on stage.
But such appearances were controversial too. Before becoming prime minister in 2014, Modi was banned from entering the US because of his leadership during a 2002 massacre of Muslim residents in the state of Gujarat.
Modi faced accusations of turning a blind eye to the slayings and even offering his support.
Even as he faces protests, though, Modi remains enormously popular in India, consistently ranking as one of the most popular leaders in the world. A survey this month from the magazine India Today found that he is also the top choice for prime minister in India, despite slipping approval ratings.
Divided diaspora
Still, outreach campaigns to rehabilitate the image of the RSS overseas have had limited success.
For instance, a 2024 survey found that, while Modi enjoyed near-majority support among Indian Americans for his performance as prime minister, 70 percent of respondents acknowledged that his rhetoric exemplified a growing threat to minorities in India.
Bhagwat’s planned appearance at Madison Square Garden has likewise ignited debate over his controversial commentary and leadership.
In a statement on Wednesday, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), an independent initiative within the federal government, called for Bhagwat’s visa to be revoked.
The commission warned that Bhagwat was “complicit in religious freedom violations”, along with other RSS members and Indian officials.
“Religious freedom conditions in India continue to deteriorate as violence and incitement are frequently used to target religious minority communities,” said USCIRF Chair Asif Mahmood. He urged the US to implement targeted sanctions.
When questioned about Bhagwat’s speech at a news conference this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also spoke out against the RSS’s messaging.
“It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly. And it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to,” Mamdani said, citing his identity as an Indian American.
He added that he does not “support the rally” but said he doubted the city had the jurisdiction to cancel a private event.
Ahmed, the community organiser from North Carolina, said she feels the backlash to Saturday’s event reflects a growing coalition in the Indian diaspora — one that brings together Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and unprivileged-caste voices.
“There is a vocal minority in the diaspora and a new, emerging majority who don’t believe in the politics of Modi and the RSS and who don’t want to see them gain traction here,” said Ahmed.
She predicted that Saturday’s event will ultimately backfire. “I’m very confident that Bhagwat will be met with a resounding rejection that he is not welcome.”

The tendency of conspiracy theorists to police others online is associated with narcissistic traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:00:32 UTC
01:00:32 KST

People who heavily endorse conspiracy theories often take on the role of online “social vigilantes,” seeking to correct the perceived ignorance of others. New research suggests that this tendency to act as self-appointed enforcers of truth online is largely driven by feelings of superiority and a desire for self-enhancement. The findings were published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Conspiracy theories often provide people with a dual sense of identity. Believers tend to view themselves as part of a privileged minority that has uncovered hidden truths, while also casting themselves as heroic underdogs fighting against powerful forces. Earlier research established that believing in conspiracy theories is closely tied to narcissism and feelings of intellectual superiority.
For instance, a review covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that one of the strongest personality traits linked to conspiracy beliefs is a tendency to act antagonistic and superior to others. Along similar lines, a 2022 review indicated that narcissistic desires to feel special and dominant make conspiracy narratives especially appealing, as they allow believers to feel uniquely insightful.
This prior research set the stage for a new question. Does this sense of superiority motivate conspiracy theorists to actively police and attack others on the internet? The research, led by Achilleas Piliousis, a PhD candidate in the Department of Journalism and Mass Communications at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, investigated how and why people transform their private conspiracy beliefs into aggressive online behavior.
“The idea for this research originated from an observation that had intrigued me for several years, particularly in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic,” Piliousis said. “I noticed that some people who endorsed conspiracy beliefs—for example, about vaccines or climate change—did not simply express their views. They would also attack, disparage, or publicly shame those who disagreed with them, while portraying themselves as people who had ‘seen the truth’ and dismissing others as ‘sheep’ or ‘asleep’.”
“This led me to wonder whether conspiracy thinking might sometimes be associated with such online behaviors through social vigilantism, that is, the belief that one possesses superior knowledge or insight while simultaneously feeling a responsibility to expose, correct, or even police those perceived as ignorant or misinformed,” Piliousis explained.
To explore this idea, the researchers conducted three separate studies. The first study included 139 Greek adults and measured their general conspiracy thinking along with their belief in specific conspiracy theories about climate change and cancer. The participants also completed surveys measuring their levels of social vigilantism, dogmatism, intellectual humility, and narcissism. Piliousis and his colleagues found a moderate positive association between all the conspiracy variables and social vigilantism. Even when accounting for general arrogance, stubbornness, and close-mindedness, holding conspiracy beliefs remained a strong predictor of wanting to aggressively correct others.
The second study tested whether these vigilante tendencies actually translate into confrontational online habits. The research team surveyed 116 Greek participants, asking them about their beliefs in climate change conspiracy theories and their daily online behaviors. This included their willingness to argue online, their intent to participate in online shaming, and how they would comment on hypothetical Facebook posts about climate change.
One post featured factual information, while the other featured misinformation. The results indicated that climate change conspiracy beliefs indirectly predicted both a willingness to argue online and a desire to participate in online shaming, suggesting that the drive to act as a norm enforcer pushes believers toward aggressive digital habits.
“One key takeaway is that conspiracy thinking seems to be more than simply believing in particular conspiracy theories,” Piliousis noted. “When it becomes a broader lens through which people interpret the social world, it may shape how individuals perceive themselves and others.”
To see if these patterns held up in a different cultural context, the researchers conducted a third study with 188 participants from the United States. In this round, the team focused on general conspiracy thinking and asked participants about their actual frequency of getting into conflicts on social media over the past twelve months. They also wanted to see if specific types of narcissism were driving this behavior. As a result, they measured two distinct aspects of grandiose narcissism: narcissistic admiration, which is the desire to be seen as a great personality, and narcissistic rivalry, which involves an antagonistic desire to see others fail.
The findings from the American sample mirrored the earlier results. Conspiracy thinking indirectly predicted online argumentation, shaming intentions, and actual social media conflict, again acting through the channel of social vigilantism. Interestingly, when the researchers factored in narcissistic admiration, the statistical link between conspiracy thinking and social vigilantism weakened substantially.
“One finding that I found particularly interesting was the role of the agentic facet of narcissism, particularly narcissistic admiration,” Piliousis said. “Our findings suggest that self-enhancement motives may play an important role in these relationships.” Rather than acting as selfless heroes trying to save an unwitting public from danger, conspiracy theorists might engage in online enforcement largely to serve their own egos.
As Piliousis explained, “the adoption of a social vigilante role among conspiracy theorists may partly reflect self-focused motives, such as self-enhancement, self-affirmation, and the pursuit of status.”
The authors noted a few limitations in their work. “The nature of our data does not allow us to establish causal relationships,” Piliousis said. “Our findings indicate associations between the variables, but they cannot tell us what causes what. For this reason, longitudinal studies are needed to examine the direction of these relationships and provide stronger evidence for our theoretical proposal.”
The studies also relied heavily on self-reported intentions rather than directly observing how participants behaved on social media platforms. People might claim they would engage in online shaming, but they may not always follow through in a real-world setting. Future research could look at real comment sections and public conflicts to see how these dynamics play out in everyday life.
It is also an open question how the confrontational style of these social vigilantes affects passive observers on the internet. A highly aggressive approach to spreading conspiracy theories might make the ideas seem more visible and widespread, or it might backfire and push people away by coming across as overly hostile.
The study, “Conspiracy thinking and online surveillance: The rise of the “social vigilante”,” was authored by Achilleas Piliousis and Antonis Gardikiotis.

Andrey Belousov: NATO nuclear expansion leaves Russia no choice but to respond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:00:18 UTC
