Study finds media coverage of the 2024 presidential race favored political spectacle over substantive policy debates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:00:14 UTC
00:00:14 KST

New research provides evidence that mainstream newspaper coverage of the 2024 United States presidential election focused heavily on political strategy and legal controversies rather than policy issues. The findings indicate that while coverage of Donald Trump was persistently negative, Kamala Harris received a temporary positive boost following her sudden nomination. The study was published in the Journal of Political Marketing.
The contemporary political environment in the United States is highly polarized, which shapes both how journalists report the news and how the public interprets it. During election years, readers flock to political news to inform their voting decisions. However, journalists face a choice in how they present this information. A 2011 review of political communication explained that news outlets often frame elections around campaign tactics, momentum, and horse-race polling—focusing on who is winning or losing—rather than substantive policy debates. When this strategy-based framing dominates, the news tends to emphasize political spectacle over practical governance.
Alongside this focus on campaign tactics, political news often carries a heavy dose of negativity. Journalists and readers alike tend to display greater sensitivity to conflict and scandal than to routine achievements. This negativity bias has become particularly pronounced in recent years. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that negative language use among U.S. politicians surged starting in 2015 alongside Donald Trump’s initial primary campaign and remained elevated throughout his presidency.
The 2024 presidential election presented an unusually chaotic cycle, featuring an assassination attempt, a late-stage withdrawal by Joe Biden, and the rapid nomination of a new candidate, Kamala Harris. The authors of the new study set out to document how these unprecedented political shocks altered the narratives and the emotional tone presented in mainstream print journalism.
The research, led by Ayse D. Lokmanoglu of Boston University, analyzed tens of thousands of articles from five major high-circulation newspapers. The team focused on USA Today, The Washington Post, The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, and The Boston Globe, collecting articles published between January 1, 2024, and January 31, 2025. After initially gathering over 500,000 articles, the researchers applied keyword filters to identify stories that specifically mentioned Joe Biden, Donald Trump, or Kamala Harris in the headline or opening excerpt. This process resulted in a final dataset of 37,321 full-text articles.
To make sense of this massive amount of text, the scientists used automated computer programs to conduct topic modeling and sentiment analysis. Topic modeling is a technique that identifies clusters of words that frequently appear together, allowing researchers to see what overarching themes are present in a set of documents without having to read each one manually. Sentiment analysis involves using a specialized dictionary to count the number of positive and negative words in an article, providing an overall score for the emotional tone of the text.
The researchers identified five major themes in the news coverage: elections and campaign frames, Trump family legal issues, domestic policy and regulation, foreign policy and ideology, and government and legislation. As the election cycle progressed, the share of articles dedicated to elections and campaign frames surged sharply. This spike was particularly prominent around major political events, such as Biden dropping out of the race and the Democratic National Convention.
Meanwhile, coverage of Trump’s legal issues grew steadily, peaking in late December and early January during developments in his various court cases. In contrast, discussions of domestic policy and regulation steadily declined in volume as the election approached. This pattern indicates a displacement effect, where campaign drama and legal scandals squeezed out substantive discussions of policy.
When looking at the emotional tone of the coverage, the researchers noted that the five newspapers converged on broadly similar patterns. Overall, the median sentiment of the coverage hovered slightly below neutral. However, distinct differences emerged depending on which candidate the article covered. Articles mentioning Trump were consistently negative throughout most of the pre-election period.
Articles mentioning Harris, or both Biden and Harris, trended in a slightly positive direction. Harris received a noticeable positive bump in coverage following the Democratic National Convention and the vice-presidential debate. This temporary boost aligns with the concept of a post-nomination honeymoon effect, where newly introduced or barrier-breaking candidates receive more favorable, optimistic coverage in their early days on the national ticket.
Interestingly, articles that mentioned both Democratic and Republican candidates were persistently negative, suggesting that when journalists write about both sides in the same article, they usually focus on partisan conflict and adversarial attacks.
The findings offer a detailed look at mainstream media narratives, but the researchers noted a few limitations to their work. The analysis focused exclusively on five major newspapers that generally lean toward the political center or center-left. Because the study excluded right-leaning outlets, the results might not capture the full spectrum of the American media diet.
Additionally, the automated tool used to measure sentiment relies on counting specific words, which means it can miss complex rhetorical devices like sarcasm, subtext, or strategic ambiguity. The researchers also filtered their articles by searching for specific candidate names. Articles that discussed broad political platforms or policies without naming Biden, Harris, or Trump directly were excluded, which could have artificially lowered the amount of policy coverage detected in the dataset. Future research could expand on this work by using advanced language models capable of understanding context and nuance, or by linking news publication data with social media metrics to see how readers amplify different types of political stories.
The study, “An Overview of Media Coverage Shifts Before and After the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election,” was authored by Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Ananya Gupta, Tess Hemmila, Amira Jadoon, Bart Knijnenburg, and Arie Perliger.

Dozens of Israeli settlers attack flashpoint West Bank village

====================================================================================================

With hundreds dead and thousands missing, Nepal-Tibet flood nightmare may not be over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:39:30 UTC
23:39:30 KST

As the scale of the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet continues to emerge, countries in the region are offering assistance and officials in Kathmandu estimate that rebuilding could cost $4 billion to $5 billion.
Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters on Saturday that the figure was only a preliminary estimate.
“This is just an estimate. Loss and damage is being assessed,” he said.
Nepal, meanwhile, suspended search and rescue operations Saturday because of poor weather. Authorities are continuing to monitor two lakes upstream, including one formed by the flooding that began overflowing Friday.
Nepalese officials warned that the lakes pose a continuing flood risk. A Chinese government geological hazards expert said more than 100 glacial lakes are scattered across the region and could also pose a significant threat.
Reuters reported that at least 675 people have been killed in Nepal and seven in Tibet. About 3,000 people remain missing, including roughly 2,426 in Nepal.
With rescue operations temporarily halted by the weather, Nepalese authorities are focusing largely on transporting survivors to the capital, Kathmandu.
Nepal’s foreign minister said the country does not need additional assistance with search and rescue operations but does need help extracting people trapped in tunnels, restoring transportation and communications where bridges have been destroyed, identifying bodies, conducting DNA testing and storing bodies for extended periods.
“We have already made requests for such specialised services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how,” he told Reuters overnight.
China has called for international cooperation, while India sent three flights carrying about 60 metric tons of aid, including blankets, medicine and water purification tablets.
India is also planning to send a tunnel rescue team and a medical team and has offered its disaster response force and technical teams to assist with reconstruction.
‘Our world turned upside down’
Families around the world are closely following the search for people missing in the disaster, many of whom are foreign tourists who had been traveling in the region.
“We don’t know anything,” Mukti Patel, a Virginia resident whose father, sister, brother-in-law and her brother-in-law’s mother disappeared in the flash floods, told The Associated Press.
Patel knows the hotel where her relatives were staying was badly damaged but is holding out hope that they survived.
Sanket Pandey, the head of a company that organizes tours in the region, told the AP that 40 travelers and seven tour guides who had traveled to the area were missing. The company, which has an office in Baltimore, had organized a two-week trip to the region. Families are now trying to gather any information they can.
“It’s really difficult to have nothing,” Pandey said.
Jiwan Jyoti, a 50-year-old U.S. citizen from Massachusetts, was traveling with the group and is among those missing.
“They had stopped in Timure, Nepal, before they were set to leave for a pilgrimage to Mount Kailashin Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others,” a friend said.
Jyoti called her family while eating breakfast Wednesday and preparing to cross the border into Tibet.
Her friend said the call ended “at around 8:40 a.m. local time in Nepal, and then I think around 8:45, this flash floods came, and then our world turned upside down.”
She later learned that the hotel where Jyoti had been staying — and where Apple’s Find My app last recorded her location — had been completely destroyed.
“She was essentially almost in the epicenter over there,” the friend said.
Vaasavi Unnava believed her parents had already crossed into Tibet with the same tour group when she learned of the flooding.
“I was not really that worried, but I just sent them a text like to be sure,” she said.
The WhatsApp message was never delivered.
Her parents had set out on a retirement trip and were excited about spending two months with family in India after climbing Mount Kailash. The California couple are among dozens of U.S. citizens reported missing in the floods.
“They were so, so excited. My dad was talking about finally getting to spend time with his mother,” Unava said.
Video circulated on Chinese social media over the past day appeared to capture the collapse of part of the glacier that triggered the catastrophic flooding.
The drone footage was recorded at an altitude of more than 7,200 meters (23,600 feet) above sea level. Amid clouds and snow-covered peaks, a massive cloud of dust can suddenly be seen rising as part of the glacier crashes into the valley floor roughly 1 kilometer (0.6 mile) below. An analysis by the BBC found that the location corresponded with the direction in which the floodwaters traveled down the Trishuli River.
Other dramatic footage emerged from Bidur, a town downstream along the Trishuli River, and was verified by international media outlets. The video showed several people sheltering on a balcony of a building that withstood the massive flood as waves of water and mud surged beside it.
Some of the people were later seen standing on the same balcony after the water level had fallen, surrounded by mud and debris. One woman was seen waving a red cloth from the roof in an apparent appeal for help.
Nepal’s rescue efforts have relied heavily on helicopters because the massive torrent that struck the border region with Tibet — already difficult to traverse because of its mountainous terrain — swept away dozens of bridges and blocked more than 40 kilometers (25 miles) of roads.
In some cases, rescuers have descended from helicopters on ropes before hoisting survivors to safety.
Among those rescued was Dibga Tamang, who was evacuated from Rasuwa district Thursday.
“All of our people have gone. They are dead,” he said. “I have no one left waiting for me. Everything and everyone is gone. The end.”
More than 3,200 people have been evacuated by helicopter from the disaster zone, mainly to Kathmandu, according to Nepal’s disaster management authority.
Customs officer Karbir Gaire, one of the survivors in Timure, a Nepalese village near the Chinese border, arrived at work at 8 a.m. Wednesday. He said he felt the ground shaking while he was working.
“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us. We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building,” he said. “I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”
Disaster, step by step
The collapse
At an elevation of about 5,200 meters (17,100 feet), part of the glacier broke away and collapsed. It plunged roughly 1 kilometer (0.6 mile) into the valley below, initially leading to suspicions that an earthquake had struck.
It was later determined that the seismic energy, equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, was generated directly by the avalanche of ice and rock crashing above ground rather than an earthquake triggering the collapse.
The movement
The enormous mass of ice, rock and mud crashed into the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet.
According to a Chinese government geologist, the avalanche traveled at about 50 meters per second, or roughly 180 kilometers per hour (112 mph), for more than 20 kilometers (12 miles), leaving people with little time to react.
A ‘wall’ surges downstream
The water and debris did not move like an ordinary flood but instead formed a massive wave of mud that grew higher as it advanced.
One account described it as resembling “liquid cement.” The Trishuli River rose by about 9 meters (30 feet) in half an hour.
Tibet hit first
The massive flow traveled downstream into Gyirong County in Tibet. The Tibet-Nepal border crossing was severely damaged and almost entirely buried under mud.
Some people described the area Thursday as a place where civilization had effectively disappeared. Buildings, roads and bridges were swept away as the torrent continued toward Nepal.
The flood enters Nepal
The torrent continued through the river system into Nepal, traveling about 100 kilometers (62 miles) downstream while dropping roughly 4,500 meters (14,800 feet) in elevation.
The floodwaters swept away infrastructure, destroyed villages and cut off entire communities.
The fear: Another flood
The disaster created two new lakes on opposite sides of the border. Authorities in both countries have warned that the lakes could breach, potentially unleashing another destructive wave of flooding.

====================================================================================================

Prague’s spires whisper Maharal’s hidden history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:35:14 UTC
23:35:14 KST

The anniversary of the passing of the Maharal of Prague falls on 18 Elul, which this year is August 31. This is an opportunity for Jewish travelers to visit the city where his name still seems to hover among the pointed rooftops.
Over four hundred years have passed since his death in 1609, yet in Prague, time is a flexible substance. It clings to the stones, becomes trapped between the vaulted ceilings of the synagogues, and hides in the cracks between the ancient tombstones.
Prague is beautiful. In the morning, it awakens from a thin mist rising from the Vltava River, bells ring above the rooftops, and red trams squeal along the tracks.
Czechia is considered one of the most Israel-friendly countries in Europe, and Prague gives Jewish travelers a relatively pleasant and safe feeling. While in various European destinations we are required to exercise greater caution in the face of antisemitism, on the streets of Prague I felt free to walk around even with my kippah and tzitzit openly visible.
But the deeper connection between Prague and the Jews cannot be measured by political declarations. You have to walk to the old Jewish Quarter, Josefov, and open a heavy door there.
The Altneuschul
The “Old-New Synagogue” is one of those places where it seems that history did not end, but merely took a short break. It is the oldest synagogue in Europe that is still active. It was built in 1270 and has served the community for more than 700 years.
Legend has it that stones from the ruins of the Temple in Jerusalem were incorporated into the foundations of the Altneuschul, giving rise to the interpretation that its name derives from the Hebrew words meaning “on condition,” referring to the condition that the stones would one day be taken to Jerusalem when the Messiah comes.
But the truth is less poetic. “Alt-neu” means “old-new.” At first, it was called “The New Synagogue.” Over the course of history, additional synagogues were built in the Jewish Quarter, and one of them proudly bore the name “New.” To distinguish between the two synagogues, the word “Old” was added to the name of the older one, hence the name “Old-New.”
The stone floor is lower than the entrance. Overhead rise six Gothic vaults, light filters sparingly through twelve windows, and the entire hall is steeped in that dignified dimness found in places where generations have whispered the same prayers.
The Holy Ark on the eastern wall is made of marble, and above it is a pointed arch with stone decorations. Next to the Holy Ark stands the “Maharal’s Chair,” and care is taken that no one sits on it.
In the center of the synagogue is a raised bimah with a table for reading the Torah, surrounded by iron railings. Above them flies the flag of the Jewish community dating from the 17th century. It is a red flag embroidered with a yellow Star of David, with a Jewish hat at its center. The flag also has an embroidered yellow border, at the top of which are the words “Shema Yisrael.”
And above it all is the attic. There, Prague whispers, lies the Golem.
Here the Maharal prayed and taught. Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel was much more than the city’s chief rabbi. Alongside his extensive knowledge of the Talmud and Midrash, he also studied philosophy and the sciences and wrote dozens of books.
Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook wrote that the Maharal had “redeemed” the teachings of Kabbalah from their concealment and made them accessible to the wider public. That is why most of us studied his book Netivot Olam in Yeshivot Bnei Akiva. I recommend packing it for a trip to Prague so that you can return to reading it here as well.
The Golem that never left Prague
The Maharal is probably the best-known Jewish rabbi today, even among Christians, and that is because of the story of the Golem. According to legend, when the Jews of Prague suffered from blood libels and persecution, the Maharal created a human figure out of clay and breathed life into it. Something like a modern robot. The Maharal sent the Golem into the streets of Prague “to deal” with non-Jews who harassed Jews and with those who spread blood libels.
One Friday evening, the Maharal forgot to deactivate the Golem, and it went out into the street and began to run wild and cause damage. The Maharal was informed of this in the middle of the recitation of “Mizmor Shir” of the Kabbalat Shabbat prayer.
The Maharal immediately went out into the street, brought the Golem, and deactivated it. Afterwards, the rabbi returned to the synagogue and began reciting “Mizmor Shir” once again. Since then, to this very day, the custom at the Altneuschul has been to recite “Mizmor Shir” twice during the Friday Maariv service. It is the only place in the world where this custom is observed.
The story of the Golem of Prague has no reliable historical basis. But in Prague, sometimes the legend is stronger than the footnote. Figures of the Golem peer out from the windows of souvenir shops, made of clay and wood, and the story continues to walk the streets as though someone had forgotten to erase the letter that gives it life.
A statue of the Maharal stands at the corner of Prague’s New City Hall on Mariánské námestí, near the Jewish Quarter. In the entire world, only two rabbis are commemorated as part of a city’s mythology with public statues: the Maharal in Prague and the Rambam (Maimonides) in Córdoba, Spain.
The synagogues of Prague
Several other synagogues remain in the Josefov Quarter, all within a short walking distance of one another. One of them, the Pinkas Synagogue, now serves as a Holocaust museum. Of the original synagogue, only the Holy Ark and the Torah-reading bimah remain. The names of 77,297 Jews from Bohemia who were murdered in the Holocaust are inscribed on the walls.
A walking path leads from the Pinkas Synagogue along the Old Jewish Cemetery. Here, the atmosphere changes.
Thousands of tombstones stand crowded together, leaning toward one another like old people wishing to whisper a secret. Among the graves is that of the Maharal.
Beside his tombstone, people leave notes and small stones. Some pray. Others simply stand. Perhaps this is the Maharal’s true power: not the Golem, but the fact that hundreds of years after his death, people still come to talk to him.
The Klausen Synagogue is the largest of the synagogues that remain from the old ghetto. It stands on the other side of the cemetery, in an area where houses of study established by Mordechai Maisel once operated and where the Maharal taught.
A Jewish itinerary in Prague should also include the Spanish Synagogue, built in the 19th century, whose rich Moorish design is reminiscent of the Alhambra Palace. Gold, arabesques, and geometric patterns make its interior one of the most impressive in the city.
The Maisel Synagogue was established by Mordechai Maisel, one of Prague’s wealthiest Jews and one of the community’s greatest benefactors during the Maharal’s time. Today, it houses an exhibition on the history of the Jews of Bohemia and Moravia, and among the exhibits are original writings of the Maharal.
A ticket office for admission to all the synagogues is located at Maiselova St. 38/15, opposite the Altneuschul. There is usually a long line there, so it is better to buy tickets online in advance.
Outside Josefov stands one of the most beautiful synagogues in the world, the Jerusalem Synagogue. After the gray stone and dimness of the Altneuschul, entering it feels almost like an explosion of color. The façade combines Moorish and Art Nouveau styles, with blue, red, and gold. Inside, colorful arches stretch overhead, Hebrew verses decorate the walls, and sunlight breaks through the stained-glass windows, painting the interior with color.
One Maharal against a hundred spires
Prague is a beautiful, romantic, and vibrant city with numerous opportunities for entertainment and sightseeing. Prague is also known as the “City of a Hundred Spires.” It is blessed with many tourist attractions that have no connection to Judaism. Here are a few recommendations:
Old Town Square is its beating heart. In front of the Astronomical Clock, tourists crowd together and raise their phones every hour on the hour.
From there, it is worth continuing to Charles Bridge, preferably early in the morning, when the stone is still cold, and the Vltava is silver-gray. In the first light, the statues gradually emerge from the darkness, and the spires on the far side of the river acquire edges of gold. In the center of the bridge, there is also a statue of a cross bearing the Hebrew words “Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh, Hashem Tzevaot” (“Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts”) written in gold.
Across the river rises Prague Castle, a vast complex of palaces, courtyards, and St. Vitus Cathedral.
You can cruise along the Vltava, lose yourself in the alleys of Malá Strana, or simply sit in a café and watch the trams pass by.
After a visit to Josefov, Prague looks different. Behind its Gothic and Baroque beauty lies another city, Jewish, ancient, and filled with memories, where the Maharal still seems to walk between the synagogue and the cemetery.
Perhaps that is why the Golem legend lives on: Prague itself is a little like a Golem, shaped from stone, clay, and memory, with a spirit that refuses to fade. Those who follow in the Maharal’s footsteps discover that sometimes the best way to know a city is to listen to the whispers beneath its towers.
The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

EPOS film fest explores fine art, literature, theater and more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:35:11 UTC
23:35:11 KST

The 17th EPOS International Art Film Festival, which presents dozens of films from Israel and abroad exploring art, literature, architecture, music, dance, theater, and photography, will take place between September 16 and September 19 at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
This year, the festival will expand beyond Tel Aviv for the first time with EPOS in the Gilboa, a new program at the Mishkan Museum of Art at Ein Harod, created in cooperation with the Gilboa Regional Council.
Six festival films will be screened there from September 17-19, with each screening accompanied by a short lecture connected to the film’s subject.
The festival will open with Take the Money and Run, a documentary about Danish artist Jens Haaning and an incident that became one of the contemporary art world’s most provocative controversies.
A Copenhagen museum lent Haaning half a million kroner to create a work incorporating banknotes on two large canvases.
Instead, the museum received two empty frames and a work titled Take the Money and Run. The disappearance of the money sparked an international debate over whether Haaning had created a daring conceptual artwork or simply taken the museum’s cash.
Naked Ambition explores the life of famed photographer Bunny Yeager
The closing film, Naked Ambition, focuses on Bunny Yeager, a successful photographer for Playboy Magazine during the 1950s and 1960s. Decades later, Yeager was embraced by some feminist movements as an example of an independent woman who helped other women take pride in their bodies, and her photographs were exhibited in American museums.
A special tribute will also be held in memory of Israeli director Ram Loevy, featuring a screening of Bread, about a bakery worker who loses his livelihood after 20 years and begins a hunger strike. The film was among the early Israeli works to confront the economic distress of development towns.
Israeli films at the festival include Seven Tractates on the Life of Bruria, directed by Bruria Pasternak Sharvit, an autobiographical work about her life in the mainly haredi (ultra-Orthodox) city of Bnei Brak as an artist and mother of five.
Another is On Her Own, directed by Bracha Zisman-Cohen, which portrays artist Raida Adon and the idea that, wherever she lives, only art truly feels like home.
There is also Dalit Kimor’s Ida’s Dance Club, about a ballroom-dancing competition whose participants have long passed retirement age but continue to dance, sing, fall in love, and experience disappointment.
The festival will also include two competitions centered on Tel Aviv-Jaffa. The second annual Urban Diary competition, produced in cooperation with the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Museum, will present short films that examine the city through cultural, personal, and social perspectives.
Then, the films will be screened at Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Museum and added to its collection of urban stories. A separate short-film competition will focus on artists and art in Israel, aiming to promote cinematic work about the country’s cultural life and help preserve it through film.
For younger viewers, EPOS will present Louisa, an award-winning production by Jerusalem’s Train Theater, created by Iris Domany. Recommended for children aged five and up, the performance follows a video and animation artist whose tiny collections gradually come to life through the lens of a magnifying camera, creating the world of Louisa, a girl searching for a sense of belonging.
Poetry Movies will recognize poets and address films dealing with war and AI
Another program, Poetry Movies, curated by Yasmin Kaini, will include tributes to poets Israel Eliraz and Hedva Harechavi, as well as films dealing with war and artificial intelligence. The program will also feature the premiere of Taha: The Voice
Between the Lines, a short documentary about Palestinian poet Taha Muhammad Ali, who died in 2010. His poetry, translated into dozens of languages, dealt less directly with the conflict than with pain, suffering, and hope.
The festival will pay tribute to Czech-born British playwright Tom Stoppard, with a documentary, Tom Stoppard: A Charmed Life, offering a rare look at his life and work, as well as a screening of the film adaptation of Anna Karenina, for which Stoppard wrote the screenplay.
Music documentaries will include films about Gustav Mahler’s years in New York; the extraordinary career of cellist
Jacqueline du Pré, who Yo-Yo Ma recalls married Daniel Barenboim, and who battled with illness; conductor Simon Rattle; and German conductor Joana Mallwitz.
Other films examine the lives and work of artists including Caravaggio, Egon Schiele, conceptual artist Mierle Laderman
Ukeles, architects Winy Maas and Soren Pihlmann, photographer Martin Schoeller, dancer and choreographer Germaine Acogny, and theater director Robert Wilson.
EPOS is under the artistic direction of Miki Laron, joined by artistic directors Yotam David Zitter and Shani Kiniso.
For more information, visit the festival website at https://filmart.co.il/en/home-english/

Who owns Judaism? Israel must take it back from the religious establishment - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:35:05 UTC
23:35:05 KST

The upcoming elections will determine not only who sits in the next government but also what kind of country we want to be. Amid the debate over haredi (ultra-Orthodox) military enlistment, public funding, religious services, and Israel’s identity, a more fundamental question has been forgotten: Who actually owns our Judaism?
In Israel, a dangerous equation has taken root: Judaism is equated with religiosity, religiosity with Orthodoxy, and Orthodoxy with the rabbinical establishment and the haredi political parties.
From there, it is only a short step to sectoral demands rooted in a notion of Jewish superiority: Those who lead a religious way of life are perceived as preserving Judaism on behalf of the entire public and, as such, are entitled to special status. This ranges from exemption from the most basic civic obligation in the State of Israel – military service – to the demand that society subsidize a nonproductive way of life whose cost to the public continues to grow.
The ongoing wars, which have underscored the urgent need to integrate haredim into Israeli society and, above all, to enlist them in the IDF, cannot be separated from the struggle over the Jewish identity of the state. Nor can it be separated from the fact that haredi control of the religious establishment and religious services translates into control over the Jewish character of the state.
Kashrut, the Chief Rabbinate, religious councils, rabbinical appointments, marriage, and divorce have long since become centers of political power. They serve as instruments in reinforcing an imagined division of roles that has become embedded in the public consciousness – a division that is not only false but generates alienation from Judaism itself.
At the same time, however, the opposite phenomenon is taking place. Outside the religious establishment, official religious services, and political appointments that are handed out as spoils to haredi parties, an Israeli Judaism is flourishing: traditional, popular, cultural, and communal. It thrives in music, literature, customs, and in the Israeli way of life itself.
Israelis have not abandoned Judaism
Who decided that Judaism belongs only to those who wear a kippah? In Israel of 2026, this is no longer a philosophical or theological question. It has become a political and civic question – and even a question about our very ability to live here together.
Israelis have not abandoned Judaism. They are abandoning those who claim ownership over it.
The effort to enlist haredim in the military and integrate them into the workforce must begin by giving Judaism back to the Jews. First and foremost, we must break the notion that anyone can claim to be the “owners” of Judaism.
This is one of the great challenges facing the next government: dismantling the ideological foundation that allows one sector, on the one hand, to appropriate Judaism as its exclusive property and, on the other, to demand special privileges.
It is time to say what may have become almost taboo in Israel: Judaism does not belong to the religious establishment. It does not belong to any political party, to the rabbinate, or to any particular sector. It belongs to all of us.
In the next Knesset, this principle must be translated into action: breaking monopolies in religious services; restoring competition in kashrut services and allowing Tzohar rabbis to operate as a state-recognized authority; transforming religious services into services that truly serve the public; turning the rabbinate and religious councils from arenas of political patronage into institutions that work for the public good; giving greater power to local communities, a greater role to women, and greater freedom of choice to every citizen.
In a country increasingly divided into identities and tribes, and one that must integrate its haredi population, this is no longer merely a question of religion and state.
It is a question about our future.
The writer is a member of the Yisrael Beytenu party list.

One person died, and six others were rescued after a storm and rough seas caused three boats to hit rocks and sink off Cyprus on Saturday, local media reported.
A man was pulled unconscious from the sea by a rescue helicopter near Cape Greco on the island's southeastern coast and was later pronounced dead, while two of the survivors were treated in hospital, Sigmalive reported.
Extreme weather hit Cyprus on Saturday and was expected to last into the evening, with thunderstorms, strong winds, and possible tornadoes, Cyprus media reported.
According to the Cyprus Meteorological Department, the weather had reached almost all of Cyprus, and waterspouts had already been recorded at sea off Larnaca, raising concerns over possible tornadoes.
Temperatures are expected to begin rising gradually on Sunday, approaching the seasonal average by Wednesday, according to Cyprus media.
Nationwide warning released
A nationwide notification was sent at 12:15 p.m. to warn the public of heavy rainfall and the heightened risk of flooding, and to advise on how to stay safe.
“Extreme National Alert: Your area is experiencing heavy rainfall with an increased risk of flooding. Avoid unnecessary travel and remain in your home for your own safety. Please stay informed and follow the instructions of the authorities,” the alert said.
Multiple roads have been closed due to rock and soil landslides, and all drivers were urged to exercise caution and travel at low speeds.
One man has been hospitalized with minor burns after being struck by lightning in Larnaca. Doctors treating him told Cyprus media he was in good condition.
Flights to Cyprus were diverted to other airports, and some departing flights had been delayed, but Cyprus media reported that the situation had returned to normal by midday Saturday.
Lior, an Israeli tourist in Cyprus, spoke to N12 about the suddenness of the storm she and her family experienced in Paphos.
"It started with really strong winds, and within a few hours the sky turned gray, and it started to rain. We couldn't believe that in the last week of August we would get such an unusual storm," Lior said.
Israel prepares for unusual summer storm as weather hits neighboring countries
Similar weather conditions were registered in Israel's northern neighboring countries, with winds of up to 70 km/h and rains reported in both Syria and Lebanon.
Israel is expected to face strong winds on Saturday afternoon, up to 50 kph, with gusts up to 70 kph, according to a Yellow Warning from the Meteorological Service.
The warning, which lasts from 2:00 p.m. until 8:00 p.m., noted that the southwesterly winds are forecast to affect most of the country, including the entire coastline, the Golan Heights, Judean Foothills, northern Samaria, and the Negev.
The Meteorological Service advised the public of the risks posed by the high winds, including difficult driving conditions, power failures, and falling trees.
In addition, the Ben-Gurion Airport, Herzliya Airport, Haifa Airport, and Rosh Pina Airport Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF) noted temporary wind and gust advisories for arriving and departing aircraft.
A High Sea Swimming Danger Orange Warning was further issued for the Israeli coastline until 10:00 p.m., advising of waves as high as 2 meters and increasing.
The storm is expected to affect northern Israel, with the epicenter in the Northern Galilee region, and authorities are warning the public to be responsible and avoid areas that could be affected by flooding.

A Chinese doctor performs acupuncture on a patient at Svay Chek Referral Hospital in Banteay Meanchey province, Cambodia, on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Van Pov/Xinhua)
BANTEAY MEANCHEY, Cambodia, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Tob Savoeun, a 69-year-old patient here in northwest Cambodia, feels deeply relieved on Saturday after receiving Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) treatment from Chinese experts, which effectively eased her chronic limb weakness and persistent hip pain.
Living in a rural area of the Svay Chek district in Banteay Meanchey province, which borders Thailand, Savoeun woke up early to travel to the Svay Chek Referral Hospital. She had learned from a local health worker that a team from the Chinese Medicine Clinic of the Cambodia-China Friendship Preah Kossamak Hospital would be conducting a one-day free clinic at the site.
After consulting with the doctors, she received acupuncture therapy.
"I am very glad to undergo a TCM treatment, and it's my first time," she told Xinhua. "My symptoms are that whenever I stand up, my hands and feet feel weak, I feel like I'm going to collapse, and I experience hip pain."
The mother of three said she had been suffering from this illness for about two years.
"After the treatment, I feel relieved," she said. "I am very grateful to the Chinese doctors for providing this treatment free of charge."
TCM has shown good therapeutic effects in treating conditions such as insomnia, chronic pain, chronic cough, bronchial asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and interstitial lung disease. Common therapies include acupuncture, moxibustion, and Tuina remedial massage.
Bun Fa, 80, shared that she manages several chronic health conditions, including lower back and knee pain, gastritis, and hypertension.
"My lower back and knee pain has persisted since 2015," she told Xinhua.
Bun Fa noted that her pain eased after acupuncture treatment, and she praised the medical team for their excellent clinical skills.
Le Chansangvat, director of the Banteay Meanchey Provincial Health Department, said that TCM has become popular among local patients. He said at least 600 patients had registered for the one-day free clinic.
"The treatment has received strong support and high satisfaction from patients. Based on my initial inquiries, some who could barely move their lower backs reported feeling significant relief after receiving acupuncture," he told Xinhua.
The Chinese TCM medical team represents the fifth batch dispatched to Cambodia, arriving in Phnom Penh on Aug. 9 to replace the previous team upon completion of their one-year mission.
The eight-member team was sent by the Sichuan Provincial Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine. The members specialize in multiple professional fields, including acupuncture, cardiovascular medicine, orthopedics, critical care medicine, and nursing.
In addition to offering diagnosis and treatment at their primary clinic in Phnom Penh, the team frequently travels to different provinces across Cambodia to provide free medical care and has organized short-term training courses for hundreds of local medical practitioners.
Koeurng Raksmiy, a Cambodian doctor at the Chinese Medicine Clinic of the Cambodia-China Friendship Preah Kossamak Hospital, called the one-day clinic invaluable.
He praised the Chinese team for providing precise, careful, hygienic, and effective treatment to relieve pain and chronic diseases for Cambodian patients in remote areas.
"TCM has demonstrated good effects in managing general pain, stroke complications, and lower-back or knee pain. Notably, it offers a drug-free alternative that can effectively alleviate chronic pain without the need for medication," he said. ■

China's national data centers provide emergency service for Gyirong mudslide rescue
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
22:33:41 CST
23:33:41 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- China mobilized its national data centers to provide emergency service for the rescue efforts in the disaster-hit areas in Gyirong County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region after a mudslide struck a port on the China-Nepal border.
The National Cryosphere Desert Data Center (NCDC) has so far provided 53 service datasets, with a total data volume of roughly 85 GB, available for download and use by relevant emergency response, rescue and research institutions.
The data comes from multiple research institutions, including NCDC, the National Earthquake Data Center, the National Satellite Ocean Application Service, and the China Center for Resources Satellite Data and Application.
The National Earth Observation Data Center has compiled remote sensing data resources from civilian and commercial satellites, with a total data volume exceeding 20 GB. The data is provided to support post-disaster road damage assessment, building collapse identification, and secondary disaster monitoring.
These shared datasets are part of China's efforts to leverage technological means in the disaster relief. The China National Space Administration said that it coordinated and deployed satellite resources to conduct emergency imaging of the mudslide-hit area and retrieve historical imagery of the area. ■

Kazakhstan’s government steps down as newly elected Kurultai holds first session
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:32:58 UTC
23:32:58 KST

Kazakhstan’s newly elected unicameral parliament has held its first session under a new Constitution that reshaped the country’s political system. The government has stepped down as required, with a new cabinet set to be formed.
Kazakhstan has entered a new political season with a reshaped political system after the country’s newly established unicameral parliament, with its lawmakers gathered for its first session on Friday in Astana.
It comes Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in last Sunday’s parliamentary election, that was triggered by a new constitution adopted earlier this year.
The session attended by all 145 members opened with an address by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who formally declared the first session of the first convocation of the Kurultai open and described it as the beginning of an important new stage in the country’s development.
“From this day, the process of renewing the country’s political system begins. … The Kurultai will fundamentally modernise the system of government and give a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.
By improving the quality of national legislation, the Kurultai will provide a strong foundation for the country’s legal system,” Tokayev said.
A new political system
Under the Constitution, the government is required to step down before a newly elected Kurultai. Kazakhstan’s government therefore relinquished its powers as the new parliament convened.
However, the country will not be left without a functioning government during the transition period. President Tokayev signed a decree instructing the cabinet to continue performing its duties until a new government is formed.
Under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which came into force on 1 July 2026, the previous bicameral parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis and the Senate, was replaced by a unicameral parliament called the Kurultai.
The term “kurultai” dates back centuries and historically referred to an assembly or council among the peoples of the Great Steppe.
The new Constitution was adopted in a nationwide referendum held on 15 March 2026.
“By coming together, our people accomplished a great deal in a very short period of time. Thanks to the nationwide referendum, the country successfully implemented a sweeping constitutional reform,” Tokayev said.
The Kurultai consists of 145 lawmakers elected for five-year terms and representing five political parties. The Adilet party, which absorbed Amanat, the successor to the long-dominant Nur Otan party, holds a commanding majority with 110 seats.
It is followed by the Auyl party with 10 seats, Respublica with nine, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (OSDP) with eight and Ak Zhol with eight.
New speaker of the Kurultai
During the session, President Tokayev nominated Aibek Dadebai for the position of chairman of the Kurultai. Dadebai has headed the Adilet party since 7 May 2026 and has held several senior government and diplomatic posts, including serving as head of the Presidential Administration from February 2024 to May 2026.
Tokayev said Dadebai had extensive experience in public administration and described him as an educated, patriotic and responsible citizen. “I consider him worthy of this position and ask the members of the Kurultai to support his candidacy,” Tokayev said.
Later in the day, lawmakers backed the nomination and elected Dadebai chairman of the Kurultai in a secret ballot.
Lawmakers also elected three deputy speakers: former senator Nurlan Beknazarov, former Mazhilis deputy speaker Dania Espaeva and Children’s Rights Commissioner Dinara Zakiyeva.
The Kurultai will have eight standing committees, seven of which will be chaired by representatives of the ruling Adilet party, while the remaining committee will be headed by a member of the Auyl party.
What happens next?
Kazakhstan’s new political structure will continue to take shape in the coming weeks. Once the Kurultai is fully organised, President Tokayev will put forward candidates for vice-president and prime minister, before appointing the new government following consultations with lawmakers. A deputy chairman of the Security Council will also be appointed to a newly created post.
Tokayev said he would deliver his annual address to the nation once the new parliament and government are fully formed.
The institutional changes will continue into September, with the Kazakhstan People’s Council expected to be established in the second half of the month. The new constitutional body will represent the country’s ethnic, regional, social and political diversity and will have the right to initiate legislation.
According to Tokayev, the process will renew “almost all key institutions of power” within a relatively short period.

Details

The pretrial investigation is being conducted under the following articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
-  Article 437 (crime of aggression); 
-  Article 425 (negligent attitude toward military service). 
It has been established that as a result of the impact of a Russian Geran-4-type drone and the secondary detonation of ammunition, at least 37 people were killed. In addition, approximately 130 houses and a number of other civilian facilities were damaged.
Employees of the Security Service have been working at the scene since the first minutes and have set up a headquarters to coordinate measures to contain the emergency. Investigators and prosecutors are establishing all the circumstances of the tragedy.

- Germany weighing direct measures against Russian entities
Germany is preparing to formally hold Russia responsible for an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig Airport and announce tougher sanctions on Moscow, the weekly newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported on Saturday.
The planned measures would target Russian entities directly and would be coordinated with new European Union sanctions being prepared in Brussels, the newspaper reported, citing German officials familiar with the plans.
An announcement could come in the coming days, possibly around an EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Ireland on Tuesday.
It remains unclear whether Berlin will attribute the attack to individual Russian operatives or to the Russian government itself.
A German government spokesperson declined to provide details, saying any official attribution would follow a review of investigative findings.
According to the report, the measures under consideration go beyond earlier options such as expelling Russian diplomats or closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
The officials did not specify the tougher steps, but said they could include intensified sanctions or expanded arms deliveries to Ukraine.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last week that Germany would impose consequences on those behind the Leipzig incident, without naming Russia.
“The German government will make perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will be held accountable,” Merz said, adding that the investigation remains ongoing and that the government would soon present its findings.
Airport attack more serious than initially described
German media reported last week that the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig Airport earlier this month was more serious than initially described.
The drone had been rigged with explosives, and investigators now believe several drones were involved rather than one, according to public broadcasters NDR and WDR.
Welt am Sonntag also reported that the discovery of a weapons cache near Berlin has hardened the government’s stance.
German domestic intelligence officers found weapons and ammunition in a professionally prepared underground depot in a forest near the capital, authorities confirmed this month.
Federal prosecutors are investigating suspected preparation of a serious violent act threatening the state.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, assesses that the weapons were stashed for Russian spies who could be ordered by Moscow to carry out assassination operations, according to the reports.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin has not issued an official statement on the allegations.
Moscow has previously rejected claims of assassinations, sabotage and spying in countries allied with Ukraine, accusing Western governments of stoking “anti-Russian paranoia.”

Turkey is no longer a cheap holiday destination for tourists - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:21:22 EEST
23:21:22 KST

Turkey is no longer a cheap holiday destination for tourists - media
Kyiv • UNN
Due to its currency policy, Turkey has become more expensive for foreign tourists. From May to July, the flow of visitors declined, particularly from the United Kingdom.
Turkey is no longer a cheap tourist destination, and the number of tourists from Europe is declining against the backdrop of the country's currency policy. Bloomberg writes, reports UNN.
Details
One of the reasons is Turkey's currency policy, under which the pace of the lira's depreciation is being kept below the inflation rate. Since the exchange rate is often viewed as an indicator of Turkey's economic condition, the authorities are seeking to contain the impact of the weakening currency on prices. The aim is to ease inflation and reduce the burden on Turkish consumers, but this also makes the country more expensive for tourists arriving with foreign currency
Tour operators and travel agencies note that this and other factors, such as the proximity of the war in Iran, are affecting both tourists' desire to visit the country and operators' ability to continue offering Turkish destinations at affordable prices.
Many people used to consider Turkey a cheap destination. That is no longer the case. People still come here and have a great time, but it is no longer as cheap as it used to be
According to Turkey's Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the total number of tourists arriving in the country fell by 3.6% in May compared with the same period last year, by 4% in June, and by another 0.3% in July. One of the largest declines was recorded among European tourists.
Last month, an annual decline of 11% was recorded in the number of tourists from the United Kingdom, who account for the country's third-largest share of foreign visitors.
The British travel company "Holiday Extras" notes that demand previously directed toward Turkey has shifted to more affordable destinations, such as Slovenia, Montenegro, and Tunisia.

Nigerian president asks US court to block release of alleged drug probe records
Unknown

2026-08-29

Kabir Adeniyi
29 August 2026•Update: 29 August 2026
Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has asked a US federal court to block the release of records held by American law enforcement agencies relating to historical investigations involving him, according to court documents and his lawyers.
Tinubu’s legal team consists of Christopher W. Carmichael, Victor P. Henderson and Oluwole O. Afolabi, argued that the records should remain redacted or withheld.
The presidential team filed a 16-page submission before the US District Court for the District of Columbia opposing a request by American transparency activist Aaron Greenspan for the release of records held by the US Department of Justice, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).
Greenspan filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit against several US government agencies in 2023, seeking records relating to historical investigations involving Tinubu.
Among the documents sought are the FBI’s entire file on Tinubu and FBI Form 302 interview records concerning the period between 1992 and 1993.
The case also concerns records linked to a 1993 civil forfeiture proceeding in the US involving about $460,000 associated with Tinubu.
Tinubu has denied wrongdoing.
In their latest filing, Tinubu’s lawyers argued that releasing the requested records could violate his privacy rights, maintaining that the disclosure of some information in an earlier forfeiture proceeding did not amount to public disclosure of the details or outcome of any alleged criminal investigation.
The lawyers urged the court to deny Greenspan’s motion for summary judgment and allow the FBI and DEA to maintain redactions or withholdings applied to the records.
The development is the latest in a long-running legal battle over Greenspan’s efforts to obtain US government records concerning Tinubu.
Greenspan’s FOIA requests date to 2022 and 2023 and included records concerning a historical investigation dating to the late 1980s and early 1990s. In April 2025, US District Judge Beryl Howell ruled that the FBI and DEA could no longer rely on so-called “Glomar” responses, under which agencies refuse to confirm or deny the existence of requested records.
Howell ordered the agencies to process non-exempt records responsive to Greenspan’s requests. The ruling, however, did not establish that Tinubu committed a drug-trafficking offence or amount to a criminal conviction against him. Rather, it concerned the agencies’ obligations under FOIA and whether requested records could lawfully be withheld.
Earlier this month, the FBI asked the court for permission to submit sensitive information privately and under seal to explain its decision to withhold portions of the requested records.
The agency said some of the information was protected under FOIA exemptions covering privacy, confidential sources, law-enforcement techniques and information whose disclosure could reasonably be expected to endanger an individual’s life or physical safety.
Anadolu earlier reported that Tinubu had also previously joined a request by the US Justice Department for additional time to respond to the court’s orders concerning the records. Judge Howell declined to grant the full extension sought by the government. Anadolu reported on Aug. 19 that the court set a deadline for the government and Tinubu to respond.
The latest filing now places Tinubu directly at the centre of the dispute over whether additional records concerning the historical investigations should become public.
The court is expected to determine whether the FBI and DEA may retain their redactions and withholdings or whether further records sought by Greenspan must be released.

‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:11:10 UTC
23:11:10 KST

Posters of missing people line the wall of the hospital, the glue still fresh beneath. A schoolgirl smiling in her uniform; a beaming, chubby-cheeked baby; a couple smiling on their wedding day; a young man, hands on hips, atop a mountain peak; a young girl with flowing hair, peaking out from behind a door.
These faces are just a fraction of the thousands who have not been seen since deadly flash floods coursed through the Himalayas and wiped away entire villages. By Saturday morning, the toll of the missing had risen to almost 3,000, in both Nepal and Tibet.
So far, Nepal has recovered 675 bodies, but many remote areas have only been accessed by army helicopters on the hunt for survivors. Rescuers said it was too difficult to assess how many more people might be buried beneath the mud.
The task of identifying the dead is also gargantuan.
In the Nepali city of Chitwan, the morgues have been overrun by the sheer number of bodies and a makeshift building has been set up to house the dead.
Some of the bodies were carried so far down the river by the force of the floods, they were recovered in neighbouring India.
At Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, desperate relatives gathered in the hope of news. Four days on since the disaster struck, people continued to crowd round the police desk to register the names of missing family members. Hundreds of the injured are recovering in the hospital’s wards and people were frantically checking lists of patients, desperate to find a sign that their loved ones were still alive.
In the absence of information and with affected areas almost completely cut off, many families have resorted to making posters to appeal for information. Yavraj Lama said his sister, her husband and their two children were missing after their village of Jaydada, in Rusawa district, had been entirely washed away.
His eyes filled with tears as he glued a photo of one-year-old Sijan Tawang, a baby in the arms of his mother, to the hospital wall. A picture of 12-year-old Sahil, his brother, hung next to it.
“We are numb, we don’t have words to say how sad and distraught we are,” said Lama. “Our main focus is trying to find baby Sijan. He was so sweet and innocent; it’s impossible for us to think he is not with us any more.
“But their whole village has disappeared,” he added, “so we have no hope left that any of them survived.”
Monita Nepali, 22, howled in grief as a poster of her missing husband, Vishal Nepali, 30, was pinned to the hospital wall. They had married six months ago and his work as a driver regularly took him to the border between Nepal and Tibet. She had spoken to her husband an hour before the floods hit when he was out for a morning walk in Rusawa. He had promised to call her that evening, but his phone has been ever off since.
“I don’t want to live on the face of this earth without him,” she said. Four days may have passed, Nepali said, but she had not stopped believing in her husband’s return. “I feel it in my heart he will come back.”
For some families, the scale of the loss was too hard to comprehend. Tulmaya Tamang, 36, came to the hospital bearing posters of some of her 12 family members, including her five-month-old niece, who lived in a village in Rusawa and have not been seen since the floods.
“Our family is under tremendous stress,” she said. “So many are gone, and those of us who are left behind are struggling.”
As hopes for their survival faded, Tamang said they were now just hoping the bodies could be retrieved. “If we had the bodies, then at least we could have peace,” she said. “Otherwise, the family will never stop wondering and this pain will go on for a very long time.”
At least 900 of those still missing were working on the vast hydropower projects along the Trishuli River corridor, high up in the Himalayas, which were decimated by the floods and mudslides. Many of the workers were low-paid labourers, including at least 63 from India.
On Friday, dramatic footage showed Nepali soldiers pulling several survivors out through a thick wall of mud from a tunnel in the Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The Nepali army said they believed at least another 100 people were still trapped inside the tunnels, as well as dozens more stuck underground in the Trishuli-3 hydropower plant.
Among those missing was 24-year-old Sujan Nepali, who had just finished his night shift at the hydropower project and was asleep in bed when the wall of water came gushing down the valley. At the hospital trauma centre in Nepal, his sister, Sushisha Maluwar, had returned anxiously every day to check if his name was listed.
“We haven’t lost hope,” she said. “We are writing down his name at the hospitals and putting up his photographs everywhere, hoping that we might find him somewhere. Maybe he has already been rescued. Maybe he had managed to escape and survive.”

Unusual risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:10:38 UTC
23:10:38 KST

The title of Sal Mercogliano's latest "What's Going on With Shipping?" vlog offers two idiom extensions: "Understanding Global Shipping Risks: Black Swans, Black Jellyfish & Black Elephants".
The "black swan" metaphor starts from Juvenal (Satire VI, line 165), who described a virtuous wife as "Rara auis in terris, nigroque simillima cycno ("a rare bird on earth, and very like a black swan"). This made sense in 1st-century Rome, because the only swans the Romans knew were white.
Actual black swans are found in Australia, first reported to Europeans by the Dutch around 1697, and described scientifically in 1790. But the "black swan" idiom has continued to be used up to the present day, in the sense of (what Wiktionary calls) "Something believed impossible or not to exist, especially if an example is subsequently found". Thus a book published in 1847 asserted that "Among the most refined of the ancients, an educated woman was a sort of black swan, an object of curiosity and amazement".
Black Swan Events: Rare, unpredictable events with catastrophic impacts, such as the Ever Given Suez Canal blockage and the Baltimore bridge collapse involving the Dali.
Black Jellyfish Events: Small, known risks that accumulate to create a massive disruption, highlighted by the impact of global tariffs and the persistent Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.
Black Elephant Events: Large-scale, highly probable threats that are often ignored until they "trample" the system, exemplified by the tensions and potential chokepoint in the Strait of Hormuz.
Thus he's generalized the idiom beyond swans, to "black ANIMAL", in the sense of something that people didn't expect, with the nature of the unexpected event metaphorically linked to the stereotypical characteristics of the named animal. (And maybe algae or seaweed would work better than jellyfish for his second category?)
No other examples of this style of metaphor extension come to mind, though I'm sure they're Out There.
I think that modern sense (at least Taleb's) of "black swan" fits the zoology well – I was as a child aware that black swans did exist, but primarily on the other side of the planet from the northeastern U.S. so that the odds that any swan I might personally encounter would be black were very remote, yet still non-zero. Presumably if I'd grown up in Perth I wouldn't think it nearly as good a metaphor for that.
I have become a regular listener to Sal's updates. Intelligent and informed commentary on an aspect of the economy I knew little about before. His style is cheerful and apolitical, which is refreshing. He plays with language a lot. He would probably like Language Log. Glad to see him get a shout out here.
I did not know whether black jellyfish were actually a thing in the actual ocean, so I consulted the internet and was given the wikipedia article on "Chrysaora achlyos, the black sea nettle, sometimes informally known as the black jellyfish," found off the Pacific Coast of North America, primarily in southern California and Baja. The article asserts that "Despite the distinctive nature of this species and its abundance when present, it was only recently officially described and is actually the largest invertebrate to have been described in the 20th century." Which I guess makes it a good metaphor for something that gets habitually overlooked until it's actually causing you a problem?
Sea nettles (Chrysaora), FWIW, are themselves described as "a genus of jellyfish," so it's not as if the "informal" name can be prescriptively peeved at as wrong from a taxonomic perspective rather at worst imprecise.
A business-world example of metaphor extension began with referring to the rare startup companies valued at over $1 billion as "unicorns." (Unicorns are nonexistent, not rare, but never mind.)
Wikipedia lists several direct extensions to unicorn, including minicorn, soonicorn, decacorn, kilocorn, etc. The phrase can also be combined: a green unicorn is a $1B eco-conscious startup.
Other creatures have been put to use, with startups called camels (able to survive harsh conditions), zebras (balancing profit with social or environmental action), and centaurs (something something $100 million).
The loss of metaphorical meaning of 'black' (the usual term is 'bleaching' but that would seem odd here) reminds me of dark matter and dark energy. Dark matter is generally regarded as some kind of matter which doesn't interact with light, so is dark. Both words in their literal sense. But we don't actually know what dark matter is, so 'dark energy' uses 'dark' in a transferred, bleached sense: energy where we don't know what it is.

Identifying ‘facilitators’

Millions of American gun owners leave firearms in cars, often in unlocked consoles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:00:58 UTC
23:00:58 KST

About one in four American gun owners leaves a firearm unattended in a vehicle at least occasionally, according to new research published in Injury Epidemiology. The study suggests that concerns about personal safety, everyday convenience, and laws prohibiting guns inside public establishments frequently prompt owners to leave weapons in cars. Most of these firearms are handguns placed in easily accessible spots like center consoles and glove compartments rather than locked vehicle safes.
Over the past decade, carrying firearms outside the home has grown increasingly common across the United States. For instance, a 2022 study estimated that about 16 million American adults carried a loaded handgun on a monthly basis, roughly doubling estimates from just a few years earlier.
At the same time, personal safety concerns often guide how individuals transport and store their weapons. Evidence from a 2023 study across five states indicated that people who felt heightened personal threat or viewed their neighborhoods as unsafe carried firearms more often and were more prone to keeping them in accessible, unsecure places.
This widespread carrying has coincided with parked cars becoming a leading source of stolen weapons nationwide. Stolen firearms present substantial public safety risks; a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 showed that stolen guns are nearly nine times more likely than legally retained weapons to later be recovered by law enforcement at crime scenes. Despite these risks, nationwide information about how often gun owners leave weapons in empty vehicles, where they place them, and why they do so has remained limited.
“In 2023, I was selected as a research partner for the Project Safe Neighborhoods program, collaborating with the San Antonio Police Department and federal partners, including the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and the US Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas, on violent crime reduction initiatives,” said lead author Alexander Testa, an associate professor and holder of the Blair Justice, Ph.D. Professorship in Mind Body Medicine and Public Health at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston School of Public Health.
“During one of our first meetings, we discussed the most pressing violence-related problems in San Antonio. Firearm theft from vehicles emerged as a major concern,” Testa told PsyPost. “The statistics from that year suggested that nearly 3,000 guns had been reported from vehicles in San Antonio that year alone. This was the first time I had heard about the scope of this issue, but I recognized it as a serious cause for concern, and we made it a priority area for collaboration.”
To investigate the issue nationally, the researchers examined data from an online survey of 1,856 firearm-owning adults in the United States administered by YouGov in February and March 2026. The sample used demographic weighting to ensure it mirrored the broader population of American gun owners.
Participants answered questions regarding how frequently they left a firearm inside a vehicle when no adult was present. Those who acknowledged leaving a firearm unattended answered follow-up questions about the types of weapons involved, the specific places inside the vehicle where they kept them, and their top reasons for doing so.
The authors also recorded details about each participant’s background, including age, biological sex, race, education, household income, past experiences with violent crime, and whether they had ever experienced a firearm theft. The survey also evaluated political viewpoints, community type, and state gun law strength based on national scorecard ratings. To evaluate safety perceptions, researchers used composite scales measuring fear of being shot and intentions to use a gun in self-defense.
The survey indicated that 73.2% of gun owners never leave a firearm unattended in a vehicle. However, 14.7% reported doing so rarely, 5.7% reported doing so sometimes, and 6.4% reported doing so either most of the time or always. Based on national firearm ownership estimates, the authors calculated that approximately 21.8 million American adults leave a gun in an empty vehicle at least occasionally, with about 4.8 million doing so regularly.
“Each year, tens of thousands of firearms are stolen from vehicles in the United States, and those firearms can enter illicit markets and be used in violent crimes,” Testa explained. “But before a gun can be stolen from a vehicle, an owner must first leave it there unattended. Our study was the first to estimate how often this happens.”
Several demographic and personal factors were tied to higher odds of leaving firearms in cars. Men were roughly 48% more likely than women to leave weapons unattended in vehicles, and non-Hispanic Black gun owners had about double the odds compared to non-Hispanic White owners. Younger adults were also more prone to leaving weapons in cars, whereas adults aged 76 and older were 84% less likely to do so than adults under 36.
Past victimization also played a role. Gun owners who had previously experienced a firearm theft from any location were more than two and a half times more likely to leave a gun in an unattended car compared to those who had never had a firearm stolen.
Personal perceptions of danger were linked to vehicle storage habits. Higher scores on the fear of being shot index and a greater perceived likelihood of using a gun for self-defense were both associated with leaving firearms in vehicles more frequently. Political views also showed an association, with respondents identifying as conservative having about three times higher odds of leaving guns in vehicles compared to those identifying as very liberal.
Geographic patterns emerged as well. Gun owners living in rural areas had more than double the odds of leaving firearms unattended in cars compared to those living in large metropolitan areas. Living in a state with the most restrictive firearm regulations, represented by an “A” grade on the policy scorecard, was associated with 32% lower odds of frequent vehicle storage compared to living in states with failing policy grades.
Among the 468 participants who reported leaving a firearm in a vehicle, handguns were the most common weapon, reported by 74.5% of respondents. Long guns alone accounted for 11.2%, while 14.3% reported leaving both handguns and long guns.
When describing where they kept the firearm, nearly a quarter of respondents cited the center console, and 16.7% reported using the glove compartment. Another 12.9% placed firearms under a seat or floor mat, and 9.2% kept them in the trunk. Only 19.7% reported using a dedicated lockbox or console safe designed for firearm storage.
“Two findings stood out to me,” Testa noted. “First, about 27% of firearm owners leave a firearm unattended in their vehicle. That figure represents an alarming number of firearms nationwide that are highly vulnerable to theft. Second, these firearms are often stored in locations like a center console or glove box, which offer little resistance to theft. Someone who breaks into a vehicle can get into even a locked center console or glove box very quickly. So storing firearms this way carries a high risk of theft.”
When asked about their reasons, the most common primary motivation was encountering legal rules that prohibited carrying firearms into specific places, such as workplaces, schools, government buildings, or businesses that serve alcohol. Other leading reasons included wanting immediate access to a firearm for personal protection, having a designated storage spot in the vehicle, and everyday convenience.
“I’d emphasize that this is not about assigning blame to firearm owners,” Testa told PsyPost. “Many people who leave firearms in vehicles are doing so because they cannot bring them into workplaces or other gun-free locations. Only recently have safes and other devices designed to securely store a firearm in a vehicle become available for sale, and it is still not the norm to install these in your vehicle.”
“That’s exactly why practical solutions matter,” Testa added. “We still need to figure out best practices for how to reduce firearm thefts from vehicles, and doing so is a violence prevention strategy that firearm owners, law enforcement, and public health researchers can all agree on.”
The findings come with some limitations. Because the study relies on self-reported survey answers, some participants may have underreported leaving firearms in vehicles due to social desirability or privacy concerns. The data are also cross-sectional, capturing a single snapshot in time, which means the results show associations rather than proven cause-and-effect relationships.
“This is a single survey and the only estimate of this behavior to date,” Testa said of the caveats. “I would like to see the study replicated with alternative samples to determine whether these findings hold up.”
Data collection took place exclusively in late winter and early spring, meaning the findings might not capture seasonal shifts in firearm transportation, such as during hunting seasons or summer road trips. The survey also did not distinguish between leaving a firearm for a few minutes during a quick errand versus leaving it overnight on a public street, nor could the broad state policy scores capture local municipal ordinances or private property bans.
“The long-term goals are to identify messaging techniques that (a) reduce the storage of firearms in vehicles and (b) increase the uptake of locking devices, such as vehicle safes, that make firearm theft from vehicles more difficult,” Testa explained. “Figuring out how to increase that number could meaningfully reduce the number of firearms stolen from vehicles.”
The study, “Prevalence, correlates, and patterns of leaving firearms unattended in vehicles among US firearm owners,” was authored by Alexander Testa, Jennifer Thompson, Chelsea Carriker, Dylan Jackson, Daniel Semenza, and Jack Tsai.

Iute Group continues building its digital banking business across Southeast Europe

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
13:58:38 UTC
